body:
The problem is that every couple of months someone comes along and adds a completely new platform to `std`. Understandably, not every target maintainer is well-versed in writing synchronization primitives, leading to bugs like #114581 on SGX. Actually, SGX is an interesting case, because the environment *only* provides thread parking, so there'll always be the need for some queue like this one. The idea behind this PR is that this implementation will be used as the default on every new target, unless they have a good reason not to, so that we only have to maintain one admittedly complex implementation instead of five.

There are simpler implementations that I could switch to, if desired (the NetBSD `pthread_condvar` for example uses a stack of waiters and spins on contended access to it). It's just that making the shared implementation really good seemed like a good idea to me (it also might make it easier to convince people that they *really* shouldn't bring their own).

> 1. inside the loop, we need to `continue` on ENOENT, not ignore it

As far as I can tell, this actually works with the function. It'd treat removal failed with `ENOENT` the same as successful deletion and continue into the next loop.

> 2\. there are lots of function calls, and almost all of them need to ignore ENOENT. if someone adds a new `unlinkat` call in the future, they will probably also need to wrap it, and if they don't, it will introduce a sneaky regression.

I actually feel the opposite way, it's better if we annotate all the places where we treat `ENOENT` as not an error rather than treating all possible `ENOENT` in this function as non-errors.

E.g. the recursive call does not need to ignore `ENOENT` as far as I can tell, but using try blocks will silence any errors that come from that.

hmm, this initially seems like a good idea, but there's actually a lot of subtle issues i have:
1. the point of this PR is to trivialize implementing an idiomatic version of remove_dir_all  
2. ignoring this error may cause some race conditions to be more hidden, before two racing `remove_dir_all` would always cause one of them to give NotFound, but this tweak would cause such an error to occur only sometimes

> I'm also somewhat uncomfortable with this test. I would prefer if the test didn't fail if it couldn't manage to cause a race.

+1 to this. If this test absolutely *has* to be flaky and non-deterministic and has no other choice, then I would prefer it at least not fail if we couldn't manage to cause a race, because otherwise it can randomly block unrelated PRs on PR CI or full CI. It's still not ideal because then if this regresses, a PR-local try-job might pass, and so might its full CI test run, but then start failing in completely unrelated PRs.

> Is there another status a run-make test can have other than pass or fail? i would like to alert people if the test breaks.

One possible idea is to make this a separate test suite called something like `run-make-no-blocking` which is exercised in a separate non-blocking CI job. This would require some significant testing infra support in terms of bootstrap and compiletest (something like a tool state check job?)... but then the feedback loop can be quite long. And you'd have to gather consensus from T-infra, which I don't think really makes sense for just this one test.
author: jieyouxu

body:
`remove_dir_all` should remove symlinks, not the files or directories they point to, anything else is a potential vulnerability (eg. creating a symlink to an important file in a world-writable directory like /tmp, then waiting for a privalaged process (like a tempdir cleaner) to delete the file it points to)

hardlinks should be handled correctly by default, deleting them simply decrements the hardlink count of their inode.

body:
> Immutable memory can already never be deallocated.

Digging a bit by myself, I found that [mutability check](https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/src/rustc_const_eval/interpret/memory.rs.html#337) in `deallocate_ptr` is done after global memory check.
So `deallocate_ptr` ensures that global memory and local `InterpCx`'s immutable memory are not deallocated.

If someone uses `allocate_str` to allocate immutable memory and then deallocate it, it would trigger an global memory deallocation error.
But they shouldn't deallocate immutable memory anyway, global or not. So it's all good.

`MemoryKind` is irrelevant here and stack variables with heap allocations have no need to use `allocate_str`.

Yes, it is needed.

For some reason, we can repeat `?Sized` bounds on one type twice, be it in generic param position or in where clauses. It is possible that `#[pointee]` has a `?Sized` bound in the `where` clauses of a `struct` definition.
author: dingxiangfei2009

body:
Suppose we have the following.
```rust
#[derive(SmartPointer)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct MyPointer<#[pointee] T>
where T: ?Sized + MyTrait<T>,
{ .. }
```
We generate the where bounds in `impl` block, too. If we are not careful, we have
```rust
impl<T, __S: ?Sized> ..
where
  T: ?Sized + MyTrait<T>,
  __S: /* the second */ ?Sized + MyTrait<__S>,
// ^^ error[E0203]: type parameter has more than one relaxed default bound, only one is supported
{ .. }
```

It is possible to remove the special treatment here, if someday we can relax the restriction on repeated `?Sized` bounds on the same type.

> For this PR if it ends up just being to a link to a comment from nikic or something that's fine -- wouldn't be the first time we have one of those in cg_llvm :P
> 
> But if you were able to get an official place in LLVM with these kinds of things, that'd be wonderful. I'd love to have a place to reference for all the "don't emit the unsigned checked math intrinsics directly" and such advice!

I'm guessing this is what you want? https://releases.llvm.org/18.1.0/docs/Frontend/PerformanceTips.html#id10

> Avoid using arithmetic intrinsics unless you are required by your source language specification to emit a particular code sequence. The optimizer is quite good at reasoning about general control flow and arithmetic, it is not anywhere near as strong at reasoning about the various intrinsics. If profitable for code generation purposes, the optimizer will likely form the intrinsics itself late in the optimization pipeline. It is very rarely profitable to emit these directly in the language frontend. This item explicitly includes the use of the [overflow intrinsics](https://releases.llvm.org/10.0.0/docs/LangRef.html#int-overflow).

body:
This sentence currently indicates the *opposite* of that, by my reading. It suggests that `fork` and other such APIs **are** available on NuttX.

I would suggest you
- split this into multiple lines so the sentences can be diffed independently
- then split the last sentence in this paragraph into two sentences
- then make each sentence make sense individually

If a PR updates the code in the shared Unix standard library support, and your OS uses that support, then it might be updated _along with them_. In that case, if your OS is listed as "standards compliant", it might be assumed it implements POSIX sufficient to execute a Strictly Conforming POSIX Application. But if NuttX cannot link and execute all Strictly Conforming POSIX Applications, then this will break your target, and you will have to fix it.

This sort of incident will happen anyway, but you can reduce the frequency you have to chase such things down by being very precise in the documentation you offer here.
author: workingjubilee

body:
@workingjubilee just to clarify, it is not an issue of NuttX, uClinux (a Linux implementation for Microcontroller without MMU) also faced the same issue:

https://www.linuxquestions.org/questions/programming-9/uclinux-fork-problem-575040/

If you want to learn more detail why fork() is not possible without MMU:
https://comp.os.research.narkive.com/DQvb8EsE/naive-question-mmu-and-fork

In theory you can implement an inefficient fork() without MMU, but normally that implementation is called vfork() on uClinux and NuttX. 

NuttX is able to run mostly any POSIX compliant application and our CI runs the LTP (Linux Testing Project) to guarantee that nobody is breaking this compatibility:
https://github.com/apache/nuttx-apps/tree/master/testing/ltp

body: Thank you for your explanation and suggestions. Indeed, during the subsequent adaptation of libstd for NuttX, our implementation will extensively reuse the existing generic Unix implementation. Based on our past experience, modifications to the generic Unix implementation could indeed lead to incompatibilities with the NuttX platform. However, if such modifications adhere strictly to POSIX standards, such as functioning on BSD and other platforms, then the issue likely lies with NuttX. Although we prioritize POSIX compatibility in our NuttX implementation, it's objectively challenging to achieve complete compatibility on an RTOS. Unfortunately, we currently do not have a comprehensive compatibility specification list. In summary, this work is still in its early stages, and stabilizing Rust (libstd) on NuttX will require a process. As per usual practice, if there are issues with POSIX API compatibility, our approach is generally to make repairs on the NuttX side.

body:
In imperative-style programming, which Rust follows, the program is a sequence of instructions to the computer. With the current documentation style, you could replace the function calls with the first line of the documentation and the code would still make sense. Take for example
```rust
std::alloc::alloc(layout);
```
What is it that you tell the computer to do?
```text
Allocate memory with the global allocator.
```

I find this style much cleaner. Of course, this is subjective, but this is what has been established in `std` and thus much of the ecosystem. Feel free to open an issue if you want to make your point, but I will not accept this PR until consensus has been reached that we want this.

There are some very reasonable changes in here as well, feel free to submit a PR only containing those.

This tests end-to-end if we communicated the attribute to LLVM. From the tracking issue ( #75835 ):
> * add a special symbol on the function which is the __acle_se_ prefix and the standard function name
> * constrain the number of parameters to avoid using the Non-Secure stack
> * before returning from the function, clear registers that might contain Secure information
> * use the BXNS instruction to return

So here we check if the label with the `__acle_se_` prefix exists. And that the `bxns` (Branch and Exchange Non-secure) instruction is used to return.

body: The output mode determines if it is valid to ask for stdout/stderr. E.g. you can execute a command without capturing its stderr, and then try to read the stderr. In that case it's a bug (the code shouldn't just silently return an empty string), and we need to propagate the information whether the output was captured or not so that we're able to find the bug (rather than just returning an empty string).
author: Kobzol

author: onur-ozkan

body:
The command can be used with `.allow_failure()`. So it doesn't matter if it failed to start or failed to execute, if it fails, and the code uses `allow_failure()`, it is able to inspect the result of the command (including stdout/stderr).

The code that triggered this looked something like this:
```rust
command()
    .allow_failure()
    .run_capture_stdout()
    .stdout()
```

We could model this in a different way (e.g. returning `Result` to signify failures of command start/execution), but that would require a large change across bootstrap to handle the potential failures.

body: Nothing much really, just that if there were some code that does `run_capture_stdout().stderr()`, and it failed to start, the code wouldn't panic (to tell us the bug).

body:
With the implementation strategy in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/128004 I don't think there is any risk of `#[target_feature]` inserting instructions. The user's inline assembly block is hoisted to a top-level global asm block, and the function itself becomes effectively an `extern fn`.

So I've now added `target_feature` to the allow list in a separate commit that can be reverted if there are any concerns.

body:
According to https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_equal.3.html:

> POSIX.1 allows an implementation wide freedom in choosing the
       type used to represent a thread ID; for example, representation
       using either an arithmetic type or a structure is permitted.
       Therefore, variables of type pthread_t can't portably be compared
       using the C equality operator (==); use [pthread_equal(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_equal.3.html) instead.

I don't think it's a good idea to assume `pthread_t` can be trivially compared as integers. I can't immediately tell if the original implementation uses integer equality, but probably [`pthread_equal`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_equal.3.html) (or a PartialEq implementation based on that) should be used instead.
author: jieyouxu

body:
This was put into question in a previous PR with a similar function. `cc` adds `.obj` to its output file on MSVC and no extension on other architectures. Therefore, having this as a helper function would cause the following:

1. Use `object_filename` to select the object filename for `cc`.
2. On MSVC, this creates the file `test.obj.obj`.
3. llvm_ar would then panic on MSVC with `test.obj is not a file or a directory`.

Now, if instead this theoretical helper was written as `if is_msvc() { "test" } else { "test.o" };`

1. Use `object_filename` to select the object filename for `cc`.
2. On MSVC, this creates the file `test.obj`.
3. llvm_ar would then panic on MSVC with `test is not a file or a directory` .

I agree that this is pretty messy, but reworking `cc` and `build_native_static_lib` should be the topic of a whole new PR.

body:
"prevent some code optimizations", weirdly, is something people start relying on if you are unclear about it.

And we should be careful about "values stored in memory", because the lowered machine code must uphold the program as it is executed on the abstract machine, which has its own memory.

And sometimes these optimizations _aren't_ inhibited, but people file bugs because the result is confusing!

body: We may be able to handwave slightly less by being more direct: The problem is more fundamentally that _printing the pointer is part of the program_. Therefore by inserting such prints to obtain introspection on their program's behavior, a programmer now introspects a different program. There's no _guarantee_ of equivalence in machine code emitted for two similar programs.

@flba-eb this PR cannot merge without this line because there is a CI check that every target file is also listed here. I am waiting for a proper ssh tunnel into a QNX 7.0 workbench to do thorough testing - in the mean time i did a bunch of spot tests.

One unexpected stumbling block was that depending on QNX kernel configuration, the same binary could refuse to execute unless this was added to `.cargo/config.toml`:

```toml
[target.aarch64-unknown-nto-qnx700]
rustflags = ["-C", "relro_level=off"]
```

without this, it would fail with `syntax error: .... unexpected`.  Debugging the binary startup with `export DL_DEBUG=all` showed that the resolution scope was incorrect (it should have been resolving to the binary itself)

```
Resolution scope for Executable->/bin/sh:
        Executable->/bin/sh
        libc.so.4->/usr/lib/ldqnx-64.so.2
```

I do not think relro should be disabled by default, but I wonder if this info should be added to the `nto-qnx.md` -- it did take me a long time to figure it out.

> @flba-eb this PR cannot merge without this line because there is a CI check that every target file is also listed here. I am waiting for a proper ssh tunnel into a QNX 7.0 workbench to do thorough testing - in the mean time i did a bunch of spot tests.

Sorry for being unclear about this: Just put a `?` instead of `✓` to the std column and I'm fine with this change. I just want to make it clear that std is not fully supported yet.

> One unexpected stumbling block was that depending on QNX kernel configuration, the same binary could refuse to execute unless this was added to `.cargo/config.toml`:
> 
> ```toml
> [target.aarch64-unknown-nto-qnx700]
> rustflags = ["-C", "relro_level=off"]
> ```
> 
> without this, it would fail with `syntax error: .... unexpected`. Debugging the binary startup with `export DL_DEBUG=all` showed that the resolution scope was incorrect (it should have been resolving to the binary itself)
> 
> ```
> Resolution scope for Executable->/bin/sh:
>         Executable->/bin/sh
>         libc.so.4->/usr/lib/ldqnx-64.so.2
> ```
> 
> I do not think relro should be disabled by default, but I wonder if this info should be added to the `nto-qnx.md` -- it did take me a long time to figure it out.

Interesting, I did not have this issue when starting to add QNX support (I started with 7.0). Thanks for adding it to the documentation.

body:
I don't have deep assembly knowledge, but I do know a little bit about the hardware.

It's good to separate out two things:
- There is the hardware that is machine code
- Then there is the instructions making up that machine code

The hardware can run in two modes: Arm mode and Thumb mode. Some cpus can run both and some can only run one, but they all behave the same way. The cpus can switch which mode they're running in at runtime on the fly.
But important to know is that the hardware does not know what machine code it is running. It must be told when to switch.

Afaik, this can only be done in branch (`b`) instructions that also have the `x` (for eXchange) in them, like `bx` and `blx`. All functions (and I guess labels) are 16-bit aligned. So the lowest bit has no significance in determining the address to jump to. Instead the lowest bit is known as the 'thumb' bit. On a `bx` instruction, if the thumb bit is **not** set then the cpu will switch to (or remain in) Arm mode. If the thumb bit is set, then the cpu will switch to Thumb mode.

This is where `.thumb_func` comes in. It implies a `.thumb` directive and gives information to the assembler and linker that this is a thumb symbol and as such the thumb bit must be set when branching to it. This is called 'interworking' and there's a bit more to it because the cpu must also possibly switch modes when returning from a functions.

Then over to the instructions themselves. They can be compiled to machine code and are done so either using Arm or Thumb representation. In the assembly you can tell the assembler which one is to be used.

When adding `.arm` or `.code 32`, it means the instructions after it are to be assembled using the Arm mode.
When adding `.thumb` or `.code 16`, then the instructions will be encoded as Thumb.

Then another thing is which syntax is used. It can be `.syntax [unified | divided]`. When unified is used, then a newer assembly is used that can specify both Arm and Thumb instructions. The older divided has slightly different syntax for the two modes. I'm not sure what the default is when you don't specify it. But I believe that when looking at the instructions using e.g. objdump it's always shown with the unified syntax. I don't know... I also don't know if it's relevant for you now.

I found this nice page with directives with some short explanations:
https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/as/ARM-Directives.html

Note though that for `.thumb_func` it says: "This directive is not necessary when generating EABI objects. On these targets the encoding is implicit when generating Thumb code."
I think that may not be true for the assembly we put into LLVM and that `.thumb_func` is required. But I've not tested that.

TLDR:

- `.arm` or `.code 32` switch the instruction encoding to Arm mode
- `.thumb` or `.code 16` switch the instruction encoding to Thumb mode
- Use `.thumb_func` to mark a symbol as a Thumb symbol. It sets up the 'interworking' so the cpu will switch to thumb mode when branching to the symbol or returning to it. It also implies `.thumb`

I hope this helps understanding! (Or at least didn't make it worse)

body:
This text is, in my opinion, either incorrect or not specific enough about the situation it is warning against.

`Waker::noop()` is a perfectly good way to _implement executing a task_ in the case where it is an acceptable performance tradeoff, or suitable for the application, to poll the task every time through some sort of loop (or to poll the task exactly once, as in [`now_or_never()`](https://docs.rs/futures/latest/futures/future/trait.FutureExt.html#method.now_or_never)). No wakeups are “lost” because the task is unconditionally awake. This is, to my mind, the main use case of `Waker::noop()`: to implement async execution trivially when it isn't worth the complexity of implementing it better.

It can only cause lost wakeups if you *mix* polling the task this way with polling the task another way (which is not trivial to do, since it involves shared ownership of the task, or using `noop()` within a future combinator).  I get the impression from https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/98286#issuecomment-2243447136 that your use case is perhaps doing something like that, but the text in this change is talking about non-async functions only, not mixing polling from a non-async function and polling from an executor.

Could you rephrase this to be more specific about the situation you are warning against?

body:
> What do you think now?

That’s specific enough that it no longer has the “vague scary warning” problem, yes. Further comments:

* I don't think the words “runtime-agnostic” are adding anything here; if the future has knowledge about the runtime then that potentially overrides *everything* about the conventional `Future`/`Waker` protocol, so it doesn't need to be called out here.

* It’s still possible to use a noop waker correctly in this scenario. In particular, the usual time a wrapper future is likely to be without `Context` is at construction, and futures are always polled once to start. So, if `Foo` wraps `Bar` and polls `Bar` with a noop waker when `Foo` is constructed, then that's fine as long as `Foo` also polls `Bar` with the propagated waker when `Foo` is polled for the first time. I don't have an idea for how to describe this sort of scenario concisely, though.

> I've avoided the term "future combinator" since it seems rather abstruse

Yes, and pedantically, you can have a future that wraps other futures without it being purely a combinator, so this is more correct.
author: kpreid

body:
I understand what, @ijackson, you're trying to do here, and I appreciate the intent.  And so it kind of saddens me to be so negative on this change, but...

> When implementing a runtime-agnostic future which wraps other future(s), do not use this function as a way to be able to call `poll` methods when you don't have your caller's `Context` available. Using a no-op waker for that purpose would cause wakeups to be lost: the inner future would store only the no-op waker, replacing the proper waker for the waiting task.

In addition to the good points that @kpreid [raised](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/128064/files#r1700481858), when I read this, I think to myself, "anyone who is able to parse and interpret those two sentences already knows the limitations without needing to be told."

That's what I think the nature of the problem is here.  It seems harder to write an accessible and correct warning than it is to just write an accessible statement of what this does do.

Actually, how about something like this? Expanding the current paragraph that says “This is mostly useful for writing tests…”, we could write:

> This is mostly useful for writing tests that need a `Context` to poll some futures, but are not expecting those futures to wake the waker or do not need to do anything specific if it happens. More generally, using `Waker::noop()` to poll a future **discards the notification of when the future should be polled again**, and therefore, it should only be used when such a notification will not be needed to make progress.

I think this would fairly well get across some useful points:

* What you are doing here is discarding a message. (People understand that this can mean that progress stops because the message is not delivered where it is needed.)
* It is reasonable to discard a message specifically when nothing needs to be done about it.

without getting further into the details of precisely classifying what situations this applies to.

body:
Suggestion: on msvc, by default dynamic libraries (say library name is `foo`) are compiled by rustc to

```rs
foo.dll     // dylib
foo.dll.lib // import library for the dylib
foo.dll.exp // export library for the dylib
```

Notice the `.dll.lib` extension of the *import library for the dynamic library*.

msvc `cl.exe` (or rather the underlying `link.exe`) requires the *import library for the dynamic library* as input, i.e. `foo.dll.lib` not `foo.dll`. So this is correct, but let's rename the variable to e.g. `library` which is correct for both dynamic libraries on other platforms **and** *import library for dynamic library* on msvc.

Please also include this comment paraphrased here. Either that, or we introduce another helper like `import_lib_for_dylib_name()` in the support library.

I think only one field of `PhantomData`  does not imply that the whole type does not require a pub constructor, so the logic is a little different for `PhantomData`.

For example, if the whole type only have one field of `PhantomData<T>` and other fields of normal types, `PhantomData` is used to represent that the type owns `T`. So that marking types whose fields are all of `PhantomData` is more precise. In such cases, the whole type is usually used to check things like well-formedness.

Problem: on windows msvc *specifically*, `build_native_dynamic_lib` only produces `foo.dll`, which is the dynamic library. But for the purposes of linking via `link.exe`, it only accepts the *import library for the dynamic library*, i.e. `foo.dll.lib`.

Trying to produce the import library for the dynamic library is... not quite trivial:  see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9360280/how-to-make-a-lib-file-when-have-a-dll-file-and-a-header-file.

There are two possible paths here:

1. We could try to use the `cc` crate or otherwise try to make our own import library with `dumpbin`, `lib` and some clever manipulation...
2. Or we could just `ignore-msvc` with reason "msvc linking to dylib requires building an import library for the dylib, left as an exercise for the future reader".

I'm personally inclined to go with option (2), unless you want to tackle this lol.

This method serves 3 purposes:

body:
> but that spawns an additional process

The time spent on spawning processes here is negligible in practice. At least, when I am working on and running the test suite.

> adds a hard dependency on llvm

This is *intentional*, our backend currently still is predominantly llvm and our test suites very much only have llvm in mind, so llvm bin tools will have to be available anyway -- e.g. our codegen tests rely on FileCheck. There *may* be a way to avoid depending on llvm or its tools for the `run-make` test suite, but I'm not willing to tackle removing that dependency *immediately* now or try to maintain a hand-rolled version that supports different flags at present (symbol reading is extremely tricky, and it has a bunch of edge cases that we don't have tests for if we roll our own version). We could first port the Makefile tests into rmake.rs, and then we could maybe try to roll our own e.g. symbol reading based on `object` or friends.

For now, I would like to stick with the simpler version of "just use `llvm_objdump` for now, it's good enough".

> and a _**lot**_ of the unported tests involve looking at the the symbols present in a compiled binary.

A lot of already ported tests also already depend on `llvm_objdump`. And yes, see above for why I'm unwilling to maintain our own version of symbol reading at present (I would be more willing to accept a more hand-rolled solution once `Makefile`s are gone).

>     1. the increased code size now should be offset by decreased code size in the future due to other tests using the same helper functions

This is test code and the built test artifacts are not shipped to end users, so code size is not a concern to us.

>     2. futureproofing allowing these tests to run without llvm in case we want to make cranelift-only builds a primary focus at some point

I would like to focus on making rmake.rs tests work for llvm *first*. We can always revisit the test suites when `cranelift` seeks first-class support in the test suites.

>     3. makes the test suite run a bit faster due to not starting an entire new process

I'm not considering improving test run time at the present, considering at worst we preserve creating processes like the original Makefiles did. I would like the tests to be more maintainable *first*.

The cranelift or gcc backends could lawfully implement the stores by introducing implicit sfences that were then propagated forward by their InstCombine pass or similar, as I mentioned in the LLVM issue, like
```
[store !nt, sfence, store !nt, sfence, ..] => [store !nt, store !nt, sfence, ..]
```
I don't consider this insane. Perhaps complex? But this would both reap the benefits of these stores in actual programs and also solve the problem regarding the Rust memory model. So I would prefer we mention somewhere that there are *complex* but plausible options here even on x86, and what is important is that they *simply cannot* lower this *directly* to the nontemporal store instructions on some architectures.

body:
The main reason is so that I can control inlining.

I put `#[inline(always)]` above all the non-"intermediate" functions in `library/core/src/num/int_sqrt.rs` so that those functions would be inlined into the `checked_isqrt` and `isqrt` functions, as if they'd been custom written and to reduce the number of function calls.

To do that in `isqrt` indirectly through `checked_isqrt`, I'd need to mark `checked_isqrt` as `#[inline(always)]`, but that would cause the behind-the-scenes implementations to be inlined wherever the programmer used `checked_isqrt`.

Along those lines, I still need to remove the `#[inline]` attributes on `isqrt` and `checked_isqrt`.

---

The "intermediate" functions support the types with more bits. For example, `u128` uses `intermediate_u64`, which uses `intermediate_u32`, which uses `intermediate_u16`, which uses `intermediate_u8`. The intermediate functions produce the integer square root and the remainder (how much higher the input is than the square of its integer square root).

I don't want to inline the intermediate functions because then `u128` would become huge. Not inlining them also allows them to be shared if, for example, the programmer uses `isqrt` on both `u16`s and `u64`s.

---

Do you think that this is a good plan?

> On any of the unsafe functions, could you add a `debug_assert!` of the preconditions? (i.e. `n >= 0` here)

I did that, but in a slightly different manner. I used [`assert_unsafe_precondition!`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.assert_unsafe_precondition.html) instead of `debug_assert!`.

`debug_assert!` looks at whether `core` is compiled in debug mode, and it's usually not, so it almost always is optimized away. On the other hand, `assert_unsafe_precondition!` looks at whether the user code is compiled in debug mode.

<details>
<summary>Altered code</summary>

```rust
        #[inline(always)]
        pub const unsafe fn $SignedT(n: $SignedT) -> $SignedT {
            assert_unsafe_precondition!(
                check_library_ub,
                concat!(
                    "`isqrt` internal error: Passing a negative number to `core::num::int_sqrt::",
                    stringify!($SignedT),
                    "` causes undefined behavior."
                ),
                (n: $SignedT = n) => n >= 0
            );

            $UnsignedT(n as $UnsignedT) as $SignedT
        }
```
</details>

body:
Don't use `inline(always)` for this.  Inlining is bottom-up in LLVM, so if LLVM decided to inline the callee into this, this attribute would then force it to inline the whole thing every time.

Just use normal `#[inline]` and trust the heuristics.  I don't think there should be a single `inline(always)` in this whole PR.

(To me, there's only two reasons for `inline(always)`: weird tricks that directly read the stack frame and thus *have* to be inlined to work, and things used so pervasively that it not inlined even in debug builds it destroys performance, like `ptr::read`.  This is neither -- sure `isqrt` is slower in debug, but so is everything else and there's not nearly as many `isqrt` calls in a normal program as there are things like `ptr::read`.)

I think that if the SOLID platform has a downgrade method on their locks that should still be preferred, but I agree with you if that is not the case.

However, I think that if it is possible for an implementation to allow waiting readers to gain access after a call to `downgrade`, that is still beneficial, even if the queue implementation does not. For example, in my proposed futex implementation it is true that not all waiting readers will get access, but at the very least some of them will win an [atomic update race](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/128219/files#diff-9a900676444ba4b5d6dc1375805a35295ad1e6fe97af126824711951536960d8R128) and get the read lock. 

If we don't allow waiting readers to read after a call to `downgrade`, then I feel the whole point of introducing `downgrade` is somewhat muted. Only the writer who had the write lock will get to read, which seems like the opposite of what someone calling `downgrade` to change the lock into shared mode would want.

body:
So this goes back to the bullet point task at the very top about performance and if this is a good idea or not.

Here I am changing the protocol such that if `downgrade` is called, we wake up all readers even if there are writers waiting. The reasoning behind this is that if someone calls `downgrade` on the `RwLock`, then it is reasonable to say that they want other people to read the value they are protecting. Otherwise what was the point of downgrading in the first place? It doesn't make too much sense to say that if there are any writers waiting, `RwLock` `downgrade` only allows the writer who just downgraded to read.

In other words, this is the one case where readers would intentionally take the lock before writers. This additionally provides a mechanism to prefer readers over writers if people want that, but that is a secondary feature.

I can add this context in the comments if that helps?

body:
This seems confusingly worded, to me.
- Ord "by definition" is a total order.
- The type variable is K, but you write `K: Ord` here, suggesting that is different from `K`.

When discussing something bounded by Ord, because the trait defines itself as "implemented for traits that have a total order", you are normally allowed to assume that type has a total order. This is discussing the situation where that assumption is violated. That doesn't really happen for K, because it is a parameter, not a concrete instance. It doesn't happen for Ord, because that's a trait, not its implementation. So I think it also doesn't happen for `K: Ord`, but rather happens for a "fully resolved" instance where K has been substituted with a specific type and a specific implementation of Ord.

So I think you should simply say "the implementation of Ord for K". Discussing it as an `impl Ord for K` seems also fine, since it evokes what matters: the definition site, not the bounding site.

Then people would not have to try to tease apart this shorthand in their mind.

I looked at the original PR alongside review comments, and unfortunately it was not enlightening as to the *why*.

`nm` flags:

```
-D: --dynamic
	Display the dynamic symbols rather than the normal symbols. This is only meaningful for dynamic objects, such as certain types of shared libraries. 

-g: --extern-only
	Show only external symbols

-gU: --extern-only --defined-only
	Display only defined symbols for each object file. By default both defined and undefined symbols are displayed.
```

I'm inclined to say ideally we want `--dynamic` + `--extern-only` + `--defined-only` consistently across the platforms (this probably fails, but I'd like to know on which platforms that fails). So maybe something based on [`Object::exports`](https://docs.rs/object/latest/object/read/trait.Object.html#tymethod.exports).

It's kind of incumbent on the user to supply the correct flags to the compiler, including which runtimes and ABIs are selected. Making the sanitizer config incompatible w/o `-Z fixed-x18` (or equivalent) is a requirement due to codegen/ABI. Saying it cannot be used on a particular platform is much harder to do. After all, as long a user could supply their own libc I don't think you could know apriori if SCS would work one way or the other. For platforms, like Android that more or less mandate it (at least in the native/system bits, as I don't recall what requirement are for apps), they can assume you're using a compatible libc(e.g., bionic) and if you're not that's on you .

So, I'd be hesitant to say SCS isn't compatible w/ `ohos`, though it probably shouldn't be enabled by default for testing, etc. 

At some level you have to allow users to opt into things, and if it breaks because they selected an unsupported/incompatible feature on their specific platform configuration, that can't be considered a defect in the Toolchain.

(I posted my previous comment before seeing your most recent comment.)

> From a quick look https://gcc.godbolt.org/z/Yq5sMGcvr it appears that GCC does the same thing for its x86-32 linux and MinGW targets. I honestly have no clue what clang is doing as far as why it is producing two extra labels per function and `call`ing them. Aside from that, looks like it is doing stack alignment and GCC isn't - but also for the Linux version? Maybe my args are wrong.

The label-calling thing Clang is doing is a way of getting the value of the instruction pointer (call pushes the return address to the stack, which the subsequent instruction then pops off); this is used for PIE, hence all the `@PLT` suffixes on the function names. Passing `-fpie` to GCC on Linux makes it do something similar (although it uses a different method for getting the instruction pointer); passing `-fno-pie` to Clang will make it emit assembly without any of the extra labels.

From the compiler explorer link you posted, it appears Clang and GCC do the same thing on 32-bit x86 MinGW (that is, `f16` is passed on the stack), with Clang doing a regular call and GCC doing a tail call. I think it should be fine to leave the match arm as `("x86_64", "windows") => false,`. While it won't affect `f16` any more than anything else, there is what appears to be a long-standing bug in MinGW gcc where it will presume a higher stack alignment than the 4-byte alignment guaranteed by the Windows ABI (specifically, the version on compiler explorer seems to presume an 8-byte stack alignment, although I've seen it mentioned that `i686-w64-mingw32-gcc` might presume a 16-byte alignment, as compared to `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -m32` "only" presuming an 8-byte alignment).

body:
This feels like it's heading in the right direction.

My main observation is about terminology. To me:
- "casting" is a specific thing, done via `as` or `cast`
- "transmuting" is a different specific thing, done only via `mem::transmute`
- "converting" is an imprecise term that possibly covers both "casting" and "transmuting".

Is that correct? It aligns with the [Type Conversions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/conversions.html) chapter of the Rustonomicon. But this PR tends to use "cast" and "transmute" imprecisely and somewhat interchangeably.
- I think `mutable_transmutes` only triggers on `mem::transmute`, but `unsafe_cell_transmutes` triggers on both `mem::transmute` and casting.
- The crater result mentions `unsafe_cell_reference_casting`. Is that an old name for `unsafe_cell_transmutes`?
- The error message only mention transmuting.
- The lint descriptions (in doc comments) mention both transmuting and casting in a way that matches my understanding.
- `is_type_cast` seems to cover both casting and transmuting.

I feel like this needs to be clarified, and the whole commit needs a once-over to ensure these terms are being used precisely and consistently. Should `unsafe_cell_transmutes` should be renamed `unsafe_cell_conversions`?

----

Beyond that, `mutable_transmutes.rs` has most of the new code. I reviewed it and it seems reasonable, but that kind of traversal is not my forte so it's possible I missed stuff. All the breadcrumb code is quite complicated, and I do I wonder if something like that already exists elsewhere in the compiler for some other kind of error message.

body: I think the root cause why this is necessary is that the sysroot crate enables the `panic_unwind` feature of std, rather than the panic-unwind feature. The `panic_unwind` feature exists because the `panic-unwind` feature enables the `panic_unwind` dependency using `panic-unwind = ["panic_unwind"]` rather than `panic-unwind = ["dep:panic_unwind"]`.

`SelfTyAlias` is used for the self type of an impl; this is not some abstract `Self` (which is literally just parameter -- unrelated, but I'm not sure why this PR moves away from representing self as a parameter when it is one in `trait`, but I digress) -- `SelfTyAlias` instead refers to a specific, sometimes concrete type. For example, in:

```rust
impl MyCustomType<i32> { /* Self is a SelfTypeAlias here */ }
```
author: compiler-errors

body:
Yes, thanks for raising this. I believe that some other part of rustdoc is "unwrapping" the `Self` alias; see for example [`Vec::new()`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.new)'s return type. It may make sense to centralize that behavior in one place—namely here—though.

Regarding your comment about the change in representation: I understand that `Self` in trait is logically a parameter (à la Haskell type classes) in the compiler's view. However, from the perspective of users and many of Rustdoc's transformations, we treat it specially and don't think of it as such. For example, we don't normally render it as a parameter on a trait's page (though we do currently have some bugs, like the `: PartialEq<Self>` [here](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html) but not [here](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/cmp/trait.Eq.html)). So I feel like from Rustdoc's perspective, it makes sense to treat it specially unless and until we replace `clean::Type` with `rustc_middle::ty::Ty`. Thoughts?

I do intend to add information about the meaning of the type (alias, with value, or parameter, with `DefId`) to `Type::SelfTy`, but rustdoc currently doesn't use that information.

body:
> Yes, thanks for raising this. I believe that some other part of rustdoc is "unwrapping" the `Self` alias; see for example [`Vec::new()`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.new)'s return type.

No, that's not the reason. You've linked to `std`'s `Vec::new` which is an inlined cross-crate re-export. If you take a look at the local docs in `alloc`: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.new, you can see that rustdoc retains the literal `Self`.

This is due to the fact that in the local case rustdoc cleans the HIR which contains the still-unresolved `Self` path. In the IXCRE case, rustdoc cleans rustc_middle::ty types were the SelfTyAlias has been resolved to a 'concrete' type (here: `Vec<T>`). In rustc_middle::ty only SelfTyParam is retained (as `tcx.types.self_param` / "`TyKind::Param(0, kw::SelfUpper)`").

This bug (or discrepancy at least) is tracked in #44306. See my latest comment from almost a year ago: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/44306#issuecomment-1785819041 describing how we might go about fixing it and why I haven't taken it on (yet). Note that that comment assumes we want to render `Self` over the resolved aliased type which might lead to a better UX (unknown).

body:
Suggestion: we need to explain *why* we need to drop down to linux syscalls. AFAICT, we need to do so because something like:

- We need to emulate an environment for libtest where threads are exhausted and spawning new threads are guaranteed to fail. This was previously achieved by `ulimit` shell builtin that called out to `prlimit64` underneath to set resource limits (specifically thread number limits). Now that we don't have a shell, we need to implement that ourselves.

Based on cross-checking with [dash](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/utils/dash/dash.git/)'s implementation of `ulimit -p` (BSD 3-clause), dash also uses `setrlimit` syscall to implement `ulimit -p` (`RLIMIT_NPROC`).

We should also link to `setrlimit(2)`: <https://linux.die.net/man/2/setrlimit>.
author: jieyouxu

body:
Suggestion: we should document what this means and how it emulates thread exhaustion scenario for libtest:

(extracted from [`setrlimit(2)`](linux.die.net/man/2/setrlimit](https://linux.die.net/man/2/setrlimit)))

- The `getrlimit()` and `setrlimit()` system calls get and set resource limits respectively.
- `struct rlimit`: `rlim_cur` is soft limit, `rlim_max` is hard limit.
- `RLIMIT_NPROC`: The maximum number of processes (or, more precisely on Linux, threads) that can be created for the real user ID of the calling process. Upon encountering this limit, [fork](https://linux.die.net/man/2/fork)(2) fails with the error `EAGAIN`.

By setting the limit very low (max 1), we ensure that libtest is unable to create new threads.

The fork + exec is required because we cannot first try to limit the number of processes/threads to 1 and then try to spawn a new process to run the test. We need to `setrlimit` and run the libtest test program in the *same* process.

author: jieyouxu

body:
Problem [REV1 (1/2)]: recall that `rfs::create_symlink` on Windows actually diverges into two function calls conditioned on if `found_path` is a file or if it's a directory:

- If it's a directory, then a **symlink-to-dir** is created via [`std::os::windows::fs::symlink_dir`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/windows/fs/fn.symlink_dir.html). This underneath calls [`CreateSymbolicLinkW`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-createsymboliclinkw) with the `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_DIRECTORY` flag set.
- If it's a file, then a **symlink-to-file** is created via [`std::os::windows::fs::symlink_file`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/windows/fs/fn.symlink_file.html). This underneath calls [`CreateSymbolicLinkW`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-createsymboliclinkw) with no flags set.
author: jieyouxu

body:
Problem [REV1 (2/2)]: unfortunately, there's a whole rabbit hole for symlinks, with different tunnel branches for each platform. The following description is only true for your bog-standard symbolic link ("soft links" that is unofficially called to distinguish against hard links), not junction points, nor hard links.

### On Windows

But young padawan (myself included), the API contract for [`CreateSymlinkW`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-createsymboliclinkw) on Windows says:

> To remove a symbolic link, delete the file (using [`DeleteFile`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-deletefilea) or similar APIs) or remove the directory (using [`RemoveDirectory`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-removedirectorya) or similar APIs) depending on what type of symbolic link is used.

Those are the underlying Win32 APIs called by [`std::fs::remove_file`][remove_file] and [`std::fs::remove_dir`][remove_dir] respectively.

If we don't know the kind of symlink on Windows beforehand, we can check it with [`std::os::windows::fs::FileTypeExt`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/windows/fs/trait.FileTypeExt.html) with [`is_symlink_dir`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/windows/fs/trait.FileTypeExt.html#tymethod.is_symlink_dir) and [`is_symlink_file`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/windows/fs/trait.FileTypeExt.html#tymethod.is_symlink_dir). Thank you so much @ChrisDenton for pointing this out to me!

This `remove_file` and several below it is wrong (on Windows) because it's trying to call `DeleteFileW` on a directory.

### On Linux / macOS

But on Linux/macOS, we need to use [`std::fs::remove_file`][remove_file] because that corresponds to `unlink` on Unix, and there's no distinction for `unlink` with regard to symbolic links in terms of if the symbolic links point to files or directories.

[remove_file]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.remove_file.html
[remove_dir]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.remove_dir.html

---

Ah but wait, there's another caveat. If you want to interrogate the metadata of the symlink *itself*, you must use [`std::fs::symlink_metadata`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.symlink_metadata.html) and not [`std::fs::metadata`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.metadata.html) which will follow through symlinks to the linked directory/file.

> [`std::fs::FileType`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.FileType.html#method.is_symlink): The underlying [`Metadata`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.Metadata.html) struct needs to be retrieved with the [fs::symlink_metadata](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.symlink_metadata.html) function and not the [fs::metadata](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.metadata.html) function. The [fs::metadata](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.metadata.html) function follows symbolic links, so [is_symlink](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.FileType.html#method.is_symlink) would always return false for the target file.
author: jieyouxu

The float semantics RFC states "Rust assumes that the quiet/signalling bit being set to 1 indicates a quiet NaN (QNaN), and a value of 0 indicates a signalling NaN (SNaN)." so it could also be "according to Rust's float semantics".

(As a side note, I don't think `f{16,32,64,128}::NAN` are explicitly documented as being quiet NaNs anywhere, although this has always been the case and is probably relied upon in practice. Now that the RFC has formally defined what Rust thinks a quiet NaN is, the documentation can probably be updated to guarantee that `f{16,32,64,128}::NAN` are quiet NaNs, although that's probably a task for a separate PR as it would technically make new stable guarantees.)

body:
While I am generally in favor of the renaming of what the fields are called in _Rust_, I am strongly opposed to the new longer field names _in JSON_.

I'd like to ask that we consider not introducing the `is_` prefixes into the rustdoc JSON itself, to avoid bloating the file and causing perf regressions without any human-visible improvement.

The largest crate that uses `cargo-semver-checks` produces a 475MB rustdoc JSON file, and contains ~100k functions and ~400k trait and inherent impls. Deserializing that file is a measurable bottleneck in `cargo-semver-checks` — we deserialize two such files per run, and spend about 4-5s wall-clock on it.

The proposed changes in the JSON field names in this PR will increase the file size by about 3-4MB (~1%). There's no real offsetting benefit for this regression, since the JSON is primarily meant to be machine-readable — it isn't even pretty-printed by default. There's very little advantage to having more descriptive field names repeat thousands of times.

Let's please keep the JSON field names short?

Sticking a type in `NullaryOp` probably complicates a bunch of places where they're lifetime-free and `Copy`, so I'm not enthusiastic about that.

body:
Maybe I'm misunderstanding but this last sentence sounds off to me. AFAIK, there's nothing prohibiting e.g. concurrent `ptr::read::<u32>` and `ptr::read<u64>` from the same address? I think both of these sentences probably limit themselves to just atomic reads, but that seems like it prevents one of goals from the UCG issue:

> First of all it means replacing a non-atomic access by an atomic one can actually introduce UB (even if there are no alignment issues), which is silly.

from being fully realized, since replacing these reads with an atomic load would then be UB.

At the very least I think it would be good to clarify whether we forbid *non-atomic* differently-sized accesses, and how that interacts with a non-synchronized atomic access (e.g., AtomicU32::load vs. `ptr::read<u64>`).
author: Mark-Simulacrum

body:
You are right, there are still cases where replacing non-atomic accesses by atomic accesses can introduce UB -- good catch. For mixed-size accesses that will be a lot harder to fix; the academic work I am aware of generally only models atomic accesses that are either disjoint or access identical memory ranges. Currently we basically view the first atomic access to some memory as implicitly creating the "atomic object" for that range; if this is two atomic read accesses racing with each other then we can't know yet which size the later write accesses will have so we don't know which size to use for the "atomic object".

Hm, maybe we can delay creating the "atomic object" until the first write?
author: RalfJung

A fair chunk of the Rust community uses capitalization like The Book when saying things like "Are you sure that isn't in The Book?" and referring specifically to https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ not some previously-mentioned book. Excellent suggestions, thanks! I have pushed a new revision:

* Uses a bullet list for the error results. This is much clearer, thanks! This makes it look similar to [current_dir](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/env/fn.current_dir.html).
* Minor tweaks to make the text a bit shorter.

* The [API guide recommends it ](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/documentation.html#function-docs-include-error-panic-and-safety-considerations-c-failure): "Error conditions should be documented in an "Errors" section"
* Clippy's pedantic lint that warns about functions using a Result without an Errors section: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/#/missing_errors_doc
* In the `std::env` module, `current_exe`, `current_dir`, `join_paths`, and `var` currently all include an Errors section. The only function that returns a Result without an Errors section is `set_current_dir`. I can submit a separate change to add an Errors section for that function as well.

body:
The idea is: this lint only works on edition < 2021 because it uses the fact that uncaptured lifetimes are bivariant in the opaque type.

So walking the whole signature, including the opaque type correctly gets the variance of all used lifetimes. The lint currently triggers for all currently uncaptured lifetimes which are not outlived by a captured lifetime.

The idea is now that we also don't lint for contravariant lifetimes of the function. In inputs, these are covariant for the caller, so the caller can arbitrarily shorten their lifetimes before passing them into the function. While for contravariant lifetimes in the return type[^1], the caller can simply rely on subtyping of the return type to lengthen them back.

Now, the reason these contravariant lifetimes have to outlive any of the captured region is that otherwise shortening them may result in new errors because it reduces the lifetime of the opaque type itself[^1].

If so, is that in issue even if we have an explicit outlives bound on the opaque?

@compiler-errors did I understand this correctly?

[^1]: tests please

IIUC, this is assuming that the only types that may be transmuted into references are other references, and thus the set of references in `src` is a (possibly trivial) super-set of the set of references in the resulting `Self`. It might be more straightforward and more future-proof to not make this assumption and only refer directly to the set of references in `Self`.

Also, IMO the wording "well-aligned referent" is confusing since it makes it seem like it's a property of the content of the referent rather than a property of the *address* of the referent. There are different ways you could rephrase this, but I'd suggest using a phrasing that treats alignment as a property of the reference, not a property of the referent.

Same comment here about referring to objects in `src` vs in the resulting `Self`. However, this gets trickier since the rules for what constitute valid lifetimes are super tricky. My first inclination was to punt and say something that just passes the buck to Rust, e.g.:

> the caller must prove that it is sound to transmute `src` into `Self` with the given lifetimes

...but of course, that demands that the caller prove the soundness of the *entire* transmutation, not just the lifetime aspects of the transmutation. I'm honestly not sure how you'd express the idea of "the lifetime aspects of a transmutation" in precise language.

At a minimum, any such language would need to refer to the referents of references since references are valid for particular lifetimes *in virtue of* what happens with their referents in other parts of the program. I'm thinking of something similar to the language we use regarding reference validity in zerocopy's `Ptr` type, where we talk a lot about the referent.

body:
I love how concise this is.

One question, though: are the semantics of this operation fully specified? In particular, if `size_of::<Src>() < size_of::<Dst>()`, is it well-defined that the trailing bytes in `Transmute<Src, Dst>` are uninitialized?

If the answer is yes, then no change is required here in response to this comment.
author: joshlf

body:
It's documented, but not yet guaranteed by the UCG, [here](https://rust-lang.github.io/unsafe-code-guidelines/layout/unions.html#c-compatible-layout-repr-c); relevant quotes:
- > the offset of every field is 0.
- > Since all fields are at offset 0, `repr(C)` unions do not have padding before their fields. They can, however, have padding in each union variant after the field, to make all variants have the same size.

We'll need to cite normative documentation before we stabilize it. That said, I'm confident the decision here is a 'safe' one. `MaybeUninit` padding bytes being uninitialized, though theoretically that could change. I think that's unlikely, since the present discussion is whether `union`s should *always* implicitly admit uninitialized bytes, even outside of the padding-extension case.

Should that discussion be rolled back so severely that Rust, say, documents those excess bytes to be initialized, we have a secondary bulwark in @scottmcm's plan to redefine the `transmute_unchecked` to permit padding extension in this same way (it's useful for SIMD).

This is all to say: I think the winds are blowing sufficiently hard in the right direction that we can tentatively adopt these semantics. We'll need to pin them down definitively before stabilization, but that's a long ways off.

We don't remove fields directly to avoid causing breaking changes for other people. Instead, we deprecate them and keep them for a period (~3 months) before removing them completely. I'm not sure how to ensure programmatically that this won't happen, but disabling `download-rustc` due to an unsupported option (or another issue which could make things even worse) might not be ideal.

Regarding the policy of not removing options directly, I think it would be great to explain this on https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org. I will open a PR for that.
author: onur-ozkan

body:
It might not be just deletion, we can also e.g. rename values of existing options or do other backwards incompatible changes. It does not matter *when* we remove the option. Even if there's a 3 month period, the PR that removes the option will crash on this line if the old config.toml configured the option.

Of course, this won't probably happen very often, but we don't really have a way to test our backwards compatibility of config.toml, and it wouldn't be great if an unintended BC break resulted in CI being broken. That's why I suggested to disable `download-rustc` instead. 

My line of thinking is that `download-rustc` is an optimization, and if we find out in rare edge-cases that it's not possible to apply it (because we can't properly compare configs), then we can just temporarily disable it (in the given PR that makes a BC break in config.toml, for example). The disadvantage of this is of course that if the comparison logic starts failing because of something else, we might end up silently disabling `download-rustc` on CI without us knowing. To avoid this, it might indeed be a better trade-off if this crashes loudly. But we should add some comment here that if that happens, it was caused by a config.toml BC break, and we should explain what to do about it.

Based on that document (reproduced partially below, and trimmed, but it leaves out some other important context):

> ## Overview of Load Value Injection
>
> On some processors, faulting or assisting[^1] load operations may transiently receive data from a microarchitectural buffer[^2].
> If an adversary can cause a specified victim load to fault, assist, or abort, the adversary may be able to select the data to have forwarded to dependent operations by the faulting/assisting/aborting load. For certain code sequences, those dependent operations may create a covert channel with data of interest to the adversary. The adversary may then be able to infer the data's value through analyzing the covert channel. This transient execution attack[^3] is called load value injection (LVI) and is an example of a cross-domain transient execution attack.

[^1]: Assists are conditions that are handled internally by the processor and thus do not require software involvement. While both faults and assists may cause the results of a μop to be discarded, assists restart and complete the instruction without needing software involvement, whereas faults do need software involvement (for example, an exception handler). For example, setting the Dirty bit in a page table entry may be done using an assist.
[^2]: Some processors may transiently receive incorrect data from the store buffer, load ports, fill buffer, or L1D cache. For more details, please see [Intel Analysis of Microarchitectural Data Sampling](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/articles/software-security-guidance/technical-documentation//intel-analysis-microarchitectural-data-sampling.html) and [Intel Analysis of L1 Terminal Fault](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/articles/software-security-guidance/technical-documentation/intel-analysis-l1-terminal-fault.html).
[^3]: Refer to [Refined Speculative Execution Terminology](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/articles/software-security-guidance/best-practices/refined-speculative-execution-terminology.html).

body:
We don't formally verify that functions mitigate LVI completely. That would be very complicated. A normal `mov` may or may not potentially leak info. Over time the LLVM mitigation passes have become a bit more intelligent so not to insert `lfences` everywhere. If we wanted to check that LVI is mitigated completely, we'd have to re-implement that logic. Instead, we verify that LVI mitigation passes have been called and rely on LLVM to have the proper tests.
The problem with Rust is that there are various kinds of adding code to a binary:

- Rust code
- Inline assembly
- global assembly
- C/C++ code compiled as part of Rust crates

For those different kinds, we do have very small code examples that should be mitigated in some way. Mostly we check that `ret` instructions should no longer be present.
author: raoulstrackx

body:
This was introduced [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/121683) in response to making frame pointers optional.
Basically we want to run this check (from print.without_frame_pointers.checks):
```
# Sanity check: we're dealing with the print function
CHECK: print
CHECK:      lfence
CHECK:      popq
# Verify that there is no `ret` instruction, and that it has been replaced properly
CHECK-NEXT: popq [[REGISTER:%[a-z]+]]
CHECK-NEXT: lfence
CHECK-NEXT: jmpq *[[REGISTER]]
```
Unfortunately, when we do enable frame functions, an additional `popq` is required. I didn't find another way to express that this works for with and without frame pointers.

body:
In the original script:

```sh
    func="$(${objdump} --syms --demangle "${enclave}" | \
            grep --only-matching -E "[[:blank:]]+${func_re}\$" | \
            sed -e 's/^[[:space:]]*//' )"
    ${objdump} --disassemble-symbols="${func}" --demangle \
      "${enclave}" > "${asm}"
```

The first objdump seeks all `func_re` instances with a leading space, then trims away the space. The second objdump has no further filtering or normalization.

In the Rust code:

```rs
    let dump = llvm_objdump()
        .input("enclave/target/x86_64-fortanix-unknown-sgx/debug/enclave")
        .args(&["--syms", "--demangle"])
        .run()
        .stdout_utf8();
    let re = regex::Regex::new(&format!("[[:blank:]]+{func_re}")).unwrap();
    let func = re.find_iter(&dump).map(|m| m.as_str().trim()).collect::<Vec<&str>>().join(",");
    let dump = llvm_objdump()
        .input("enclave/target/x86_64-fortanix-unknown-sgx/debug/enclave")
        .args(&["--syms", &format!("--disassemble-symbols={func}")])
        .run()
        .stdout_utf8();
```

body:
I also thought about that, but I think there is still a distinction between captured and uncaptured commands. When I use the example with `x perf <wrong-arg>`, the output will be a help message from clap; I don't want to pollute that with the executed command.

When we run an uncaptured command, it is assumed that the stdout/stderr is somehow readable by users, and will help them figure out potential issues. In that case, I think that printing the command is not always needed. When we run a captured command, the user is not supposed to see stdout/stderr, so maybe it's not enough to debug the issue. When such command fails, we try to show both the output and the command, to provide more context.

> I also thought about that, but I think there is still a distinction between captured and uncaptured commands. When I use the example with x perf <wrong-arg>, the output will be a help message from clap; I don't want to pollute that with the executed command.

Rerun with -v to see more details.". Otherwise we can't know which command was failed, or do we print it somewhere else?

Another thing: If printing `BootstrapCommand` prints the stderr/stdout (based on "When I use the example with x perf <wrong-arg>, the output will be a help message from clap" which was your answer above), why are we also printing stdout and stderr separately? > Right, but saying "Command has failed. Rerun with -v to see more details." doesn't seem useful. Instead, it should specify the executed command, e.g., "Command x perf failed to execute. Rerun with -v to see more details.". Otherwise we can't know which command was failed, or do we print it somewhere else?

With this PR, we print the command only for capturing commands. We could do it unconditionally, but it's nontrivial to figure out the correct heuristic. If you execute e.g. `foo bar baz --a=5 --b=10`, do you show just `foo`? Or `foo bar`? Will this type only ever be used for creating hash-map seeds?

As noted in #129402, a future wasip2 implementation might use wasi:random/insecure for best effort randomness and wasi:random/random for the default random source. If this type would only ever be used for initialising hash map random keys, the wasip2 implementation could just use wasi:random/insecure-seed. However, if this type became more widely used inside std (or even exposed), it might need to fall back to wasi:random/insecure.

Let's replace this with something like this:
```rust
let out = String::from_utf8_lossy(out);
// The output should look like this: "curl <major>.<minor>.<patch> ..."
out.lines().next().and_then(|line| line.split(" ").skip(1).next())
    .and_then(|version| semver::Version::parse(version).ok())
    .unwrap_or(Version::new(1, 0, 0))
```
And then we can compare it like this:
```rust
if curl_version() > semver::Version(7, 70, 0)
```

body:
This gives you

```
error[E0433]: failed to resolve: use of undeclared crate or module `fs`
  --> f72.rs:13:5
   |
13 |     fs::unix::chown();
   |     ^^ use of undeclared crate or module `fs`
   |
note: found an item that was configured out
  --> f72.rs:4:5
   |
4  | mod fs {
   |     ^^
note: the item is gated here
  --> f72.rs:3:1
   |
3  | #[cfg(foo)]
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^
```

because `fs` is not found so that's the only one that would be checked for (not `unix` or `chown`).

If you check for `unix`, it *will* point at `cfg(foo)`, which is not enough to get `unix` back, but gets you on the way to it:

```
error[E0433]: failed to resolve: use of undeclared crate or module `unix`
  --> f72.rs:14:5
   |
14 |     unix::chown();
   |     ^^^^ use of undeclared crate or module `unix`
   |
note: found an item that was configured out
  --> f72.rs:6:9
   |
6  |     mod unix {
   |         ^^^^
note: the item is gated here
  --> f72.rs:3:1
   |
3  | #[cfg(foo)]
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^
```

In testing, I noticed that we don't point at `fs::unix` when trying `unix` directly and it is behind a `cfg` (the second error):

```
error[E0433]: failed to resolve: could not find `unix` in `fs`
  --> f72.rs:13:9
   |
13 |     fs::unix::chown();
   |         ^^^^ could not find `unix` in `fs`
   |
note: found an item that was configured out
  --> f72.rs:6:9
   |
6  |     mod unix {
   |         ^^^^
note: the item is gated here
  --> f72.rs:5:5
   |
5  |     #[cfg(bar)]
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^

error[E0433]: failed to resolve: use of undeclared crate or module `unix`
  --> f72.rs:14:5
   |
14 |     unix::chown();
   |     ^^^^ use of undeclared crate or module `unix`
```

If it isn't `cfg`d out *and* it's public, we do provide this suggestion:

```
error[E0433]: failed to resolve: use of undeclared crate or module `unix`

   |
14 |     unix::chown();
   |     ^^^^ use of undeclared crate or module `unix`
   |
help: consider importing this module
   |
4  + use fs::unix;
   |
```

but if it is private and crate local maybe we should at least point at it (we don't):

```
error[E0433]: failed to resolve: use of undeclared crate or module `unix`
  --> f72.rs:14:5

body:
> Do you consider a periodically reseeded, non-RC4-based arc4random_buf secure enough to serve as default random source on the non-Linux UNIX platforms?

So I'm not t-libs, but familiar with OS randomness, so just going to chime in politely. The documentation for `arc4random_buf` states that it generates "cryptographic pseudo-random" and pretty much all modern UNIX distributions have moved on from RC4 to something better. body:
We adds types to `ignored_types` only when it visits a use item, while `check_expr_post` is also consults this set when it visits an `.into()` expression. This makes the lint result depend on item visitation order.

For example, if a use `aliases::Int;` item appears before a function, the alias type may already be in `ignored_types`, so `x.into()` is skipped. But if the same use item appears after the function, the function body can be linted before the alias is collected, causing a false positive. 

Since rust item order should not affect this lint result, a more robust approach would be to collect cfg-sensitive aliases in an order-independent prepass before checking?

*[View changes since the review](https://triagebot.infra.rust-lang.org/gh-changes-since/rust-lang/rust/129249/c397dae808f70caebab1fc4e11b3edf7e59f58c7..48d125c2d13a1e98d0403f32b33835cb010bca7b)*

The ShadowCallStack (SCS) requires that the platform reserves a register that could be used for the SCS. ShadowCallStack requires the use of the ABI defined platform register, `x18`, which is required for code generation purposes.
When `x18` is not reserved, and is instead used as a scratch register, enabling ShadowCallStack would lead to undefined behavior, due to corruption of the  return addresses on the SCS or through clobbering the SCS register.
In other words, code that is calling into or called by functions instrumented with ShadowCallStack must reserve the `x18` register or preserve its value.

"Establish a memory barrier" is not the correct term -- having happens-before is indeed more correct. Rust doesn't even have a concept of "memory barrier". We have memory *fences*, but one can establish happens-before without using fences.

Compiler intrinsics are not stable so they should not be mentioned.

author: RalfJung

body:
I think that the text added / changed in 3e5a4030b5c81b6698485bdbfc5d1f5d1be3613d is great, in particular:

> The most important aspect of this model is that *data races* are undefined behavior. A data race is defined as conflicting non-synchronized accesses where at least one of the accesses is non-atomic. Here, accesses are *conflicting* if they affect overlapping regions of memory and at least one of them is a write. They are *non-synchronized* if neither of them *happens-before* the other, according to the happens-before order of the memory model.

I'm worried that removing those concrete requirements from `UnsafeCell`'s documentation itself, and adding indirection by referring to `core::sync::atomic`, makes it harder to reason about `UnsafeCell`'s particular semantics though. I do see the appeal of de-duplicating this documentation though.
author: lschuermann

body: The semantics are not particular for `UnsafeCell` though. Rust has at least two ways of providing shared mutable state: via raw pointers, and via `UnsafeCell`. body:
This PR implements a heuristic which disables two things that are currently being performed on the HIR when we have expressions that involve place-like expressions that point to `!`. Specifically, it will:

1. Disable the `NeverToAny` coercion we implicitly insert.
2. Disable the logic which considers the expression to diverge, which affects the type returned by the containing block.

We do those IF the expression is a place-like expression (locals, statics, field projections, index operations, and deref operations), and if the parent expression is either:
1. the LHS of an assignment
2. AddrOf
3. A match or let IF all of the *patterns consitute a read*

And finally, a pattern currently is considered to constitute a read UNLESS it is a wildcard or a OR of wildcards. All other patterns are considered currently to constitute a read. Specifically, because `NeverToAny` is a coercion performed on a *value* and not a *place*, `Struct { .. }` on a `!` type must be a coercion currently. This is already considered UB by [miri](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2021&gist=daf3a2246433fe43fdc07d1389c276c9).


That means it does not affect the preexisting UB in this case:

```
let Struct { .. } = *never_ptr;
```

Even though it's likely up for debate, it almost certainly causes inference changes which I do *NOT* want to fix in this PR.

The "not so egregiously unsound" case is basically the last example I gave, since that is arguably *not* even unsound but just regular UB because users already need to accept that they're doing sketchy stuff by wrapping their code in `unsafe {}`, and the fact that the coercion there is implicitly occurring is kinda just 🤷.

Recall that I'm primarily motivated by trying to make `&raw *ptr` always safe, and none of this affects that. The only stuff that's "up for debate" here is just the semantics surrounding pattern matching, which I think are probably incredibly rare, already *more* UB than they are than after this PR, and are easily refined later.

body:
Absolutely. 
For example the [chown(2) manpage](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/chown.2.html) says:

> When the owner or group of an executable file is changed by an
       unprivileged user, the S_ISUID and S_ISGID mode bits are cleared.
       POSIX does not specify whether this also should happen when root
       does the chown(); the Linux behavior depends on the kernel
       version, and since Linux 2.2.13, root is treated like other
       users.  

> In case of a non-group-executable file (i.e., one for
       which the S_IXGRP bit is not set) the S_ISGID bit indicates
       mandatory locking, and is not cleared by a chown().

> When the owner or group of an executable file is changed (by any
       user), all capability sets for the file are cleared.

And as you properly quoted [POSIX](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/chown.html) says:

> Unless chown is invoked by a process with appropriate privileges, the set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits of a regular file shall be cleared upon successful completion; the set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits of other file types may be cleared.

I have considered to quote any of those but that would've been excessive for this pretty and short help page, but linking any of them (especially the first) may be indeed useful.

`align_present_note` and `align_note` are mutually exclusive, and both are only conditional on `self.tcx.features().fn_align`. I'd prefer if you represent this with an:

``` 
#[derive(Subdiagnostic)]
enum FnAlignSuggestion {
    #[note(passes_align_present_note)]
    OnlyAlign,
    #[note(passes_align_note)]
    SupportsAlign,
}
```

And then using `Option<FnAlignSuggestion>`. This avoid needing to add *two* fields to every diagnostic, and needing to repeat the note several times in the fluent grammar.

This is kinda unrelated to your change here, though -- I'd somewhat rather you break this into a separate PR so we can refine it separately.
