body:
I added some more documentation to the code, does it look better to you?
I also have https://enzyme.mit.edu/rust/rev.html and https://enzyme.mit.edu/rust/fwd.html for the user facing explanation. 

Generally, Forward and Reverse mode are the two fundamental variants of autodiff and based on Jacobian-Vector Products (JVP) or Vector-Jacobian Products (VJP) from math, and I wouldn't want to go deeper into mathematics here, but everyone working on AD will have heard those terms. Either way, knowing the math won't help much here:

They are implemented quite differently both in general and in Enzyme, so they come with both subtle differences and with explicit usage implications. I tried to make the subtle differences obvious by using different names during forward and reverse mode, i.e. Duplicated vs Dual, even though they lower to the same name for Enzyme. I also added warnings about a difference to my user docs at the bottom of this [page](https://enzyme.mit.edu/rust/rev.html).

Which combinations of modes and activities are allowed is dictated by Enzyme core and unfortunately mostly undocumentated and implied. I have pushed for adding assertions wherever I got something wrong myself and added a lot of checks here to make sure I catch usage errors before enzyme panics, but there is no higher explanation as to why some combinations are allowed beyond "that's what enzyme core implements". So the logic shouldn't be changed without anyone from Enzyme core reviewing. I keep pushing for better enzyme core docs to help with that, but it's a slow process, so I focus on Rust docs. As part of the t-lang experiment, we might experiment with more extensive wrappers around Enzyme, or with adding support for other usage patterns.

body:
That's the bane of my existence. :D Enzyme uses a type layout representation which is suboptimal, it should move over to type trie's, but another student and I both gave up on our refactor PRs and the Enzyme core Lead dev also isn't actively working this. Luckily there are some AD users which seem to have the resources to eventually rewrite the whole typetree infrastructure, so I consider it just an implementation detail.

In less dramatic, `-1` in Enzyme speech means everywhere.
that is `{0:-1: Float}` means at index 0 you have a ptr, if you dereference it it will be floats everywhere. Thus `* f32`.
If you have `{-1:int}` it means int's everywhere, e.g. `[i32; N]`.
`{0:-1:-1 float}` then means one pointer at offset 0, if you dereference it there will be only pointers, if you dereference these new pointers they will point to array of floats.
Generally, it allows byte-specific descriptions.

This design has no way of handling recursive datastructures, it skips things that have more than 5 indirections and there are some hacks to make it handle gaps in layouts, as well as other issues with it. If Enzyme is slow at compile time than this is usually the culprit. Also it should be extended at some point to make use of const/mut knowledge, right now that get's lost once we have more than one indirection. To be fair I find it pretty cool that Enzyme is already so extremely fast while leaving some information like here still unused.

The middle-end PR will include tests for typetrees, since that's where we construct them.
I'll add this also to the docs, so I can link to them next time.

body:
It's not a bug, it's a feature! And a cool one on top, which e.g. JAX doesn't support to this extend.

If you have two numerical solvers that use derivatives of different arguments for their optimizations, you can just generate df_dx and df_dy as two different functions with different activities for autodiff. You can have a single function that computes derivatives with respect to both arguments, but than you just waste compute time when you don't use both in all cases.

Or if you have vector based functions and don't know at compile time how large input and output dimensions will be, then you can create df_fwd and df_rev and decide at runtime which of the two to call to get the best performance.

There aren't much doc comments around here but I have it described in the docs, so I instead added a testcase for multiple autodiff applications.

looking at this I realized that there's something else going on here. The constant starts out as unevaluated and we are able to evaluate it successfully even though it uses a type error as the expected type. We tend to bail in const eval if typeck encountered a type error: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/9b82580c7347f800c2550e6719e4218a60a80b28/compiler/rustc_const_eval/src/interpret/eval_context.rs#L255-L266

So imo the actual issue is that we don't taint the MIR body even though its expected return type is a type error. We should eagerly taint the infcx using `set_tainted_by_errors` in `typeck_with_fallback` if the expected type is an error. cc @oli-obk as you may be aware of a more general approach to taint the MIR body here

> can you add a comment explaining what "depth" is

Will do.

> I guess assoc types want the info from their trait and everything else wants it from itself

I'd like to clarify: On main, we already "accept" `AssocTy` but only at depth `1` (thereby setting the container to the corresp. trait). On my branch we now also "accept" `AssocTy` at depth 0 (thereby setting the container to itself).

`AssocTy@depth=1` is necessary for resolving obj lt defs in the trait ref. `<A as TraitRef<B>>::AssocTy<C>` essentially gets represented as ``QPath(Some(`A`), [`TraitRef<B>`, `AssocTy<C>`])`` in the HIR. Given such a qpath, we're reaching both `AssocTy@1` and `AssocTy@0` (it doesn't reach `Trait@0` since the overall resolution of the path is `AssocTy`).

> but that doesn't explain variant, with enums you can have generic args both on the enum and on the variant

That is indeed odd and should be rectified soon (not in this PR tho imo). However, IINM this issue cannot be observed at the moment thanks to a different bug (#108224). AFAICT, in this context `DefKind::Variant` can only be reached by "braced enum constructions" `…V { … }` as unit & tuple constructions will have `DefKind::Ctor(Variant, Const | Fn)`. Now, due to aforesaid bug (concerning lifetime elision, I think) (#108224), `E::<'a, …>::V { … }` gets rejected (it gets expanded to `E::<'a, …>::V::<'_, …> { … }` which later gets rejected by HIR ty lowering for obvious reasons), so we can "assume" `E::V::<'a, …> {}` here (i.e., only `Variant@0` bears args, never `Variant@1`) (until that bug is fixed).

(Note that even if we stopped computing obj lt defs in bodies (as suggested by you and with which I agree), this issue is still relevant for (m)GCA under which `Variant | Ctor(Variant, Const | Fn)` (ref'ing lifetime args & trait object types) can legally appear in item signatures / contexts without inference (edit: conditions apply)).

> what are the cases where this change goes from indeterminate to pass-through due to this change?

I'm not sure I fully understand the question, pass-through whereto? I don't think there are any such cases.

1. If the "indeterminacy scope" is inside of the self type (pseudo: `<INDET<dyn Inner> as Outer<'r>>::INELIGIBLE`[^1]), then the inner indeterminacy prevails / shadows any potential outer obj lt defs
   * meaning: indeterminate → indeterminate
2. If the "indeterminacy scope" is outside of the resolved (ineligible) projection (pseudo: `INDET<<dyn Inner as Outer<'r>>::INELIGIBLE>`[^1]) then we'll "pass through to" the "indeterminacy" … but that's already what happens on stable&main where resolved projections are always pass through wrt. object lifetime defaulting
   * meaning: indeterminate → indeterminate

Of course, "pass-through to indeterminate" is possible and so is "indeterminate to check-pass" (if the container is eligible) but that's probably not what you meant.

[^1]: `INDET` magically renders the object lifetime default indeterminate and `INELIGIBLE` is not an eligible container.

body:
Could you clarify? Which semantics would you desire?

AFAICT, there are 5 options for how we could make associated type bindings behave: The associated type binding could...

1. ...*artificially* induce "indeterminacy" unconditionally
   * i.e., reject implicit object lifetimes in item signatures
2. ...*artificially* induce `'static` unconditionally
3. ...induce a lifetime default that's determined by the item bounds
   * here that would be `'static` since OLD(`Foo::Item`) would be `Empty` which turns into `'static` in item signatures
   * unlikely to be implemented anytime soon since RBV & HIR ty lowering would need to be consolidated or be able to interlock smh.
   * not sure if it's "desirable" but it's consistent / not surprising:
     * **type arguments** induce a default determined by the **parameter bounds**
     * **assoc type bindings** would induce a default determined by the **item bounds**
4. ...not induce any object lifetime default
   * aka it's pass-through
   * here that would mean elab'ing `dyn Bar` to `dyn Bar + 'a` since it'd take on the default induced by the outer `&`
   * that'd be surprising I think à la "*why are type arguments 'solid' (not pass through) but assoc type bindings are not despite being in the same `<…>` list?*"
   * (although I have to admit that we do already have containers on stable that "look" eligible but actually aren't (apart from the things that are fixed in this PR, of course), most notably tuple type constructors which are pass-through contrary to ADTs (`Solo<·>` != `(·,)` wrt. obj lt defaulting); still, using that as a counterargument would probably be a stretch)
5. ...*artificially* induce *indeterminacy" if any generic arg list contains lifetime args, otherwise *artificially* induce `'static`
   * that's the behavior on main, stable & this branch
   * it's a HACK for reservation purposes (namely transitioning to option (3))

body:
I feel like this question could be asked of most of the generic floating-point docs currently attached to the `f32` primitive type: it seems to have become the de-facto place for documentation that applies to all floating-point numbers, with all the other floating-point types pointing to it. This makes less sense now that `f16` and `f128` are being added, as `f32` is no longer the smallest floating-point type. Unfortunately there isn't any `float` module to attach the documentation to; I guess the `std::num` module could hold it (in the same way that `std::fmt` has the documentation for format strings that are used by several macros), with the floating-point primitive types all linking to that module. If keeping the generic floating-point documentation attached to one of the primitive types is desired (or the least-bad option), I think it would make most sense to move it to `f64`: as the fallback floating point type used for literals where no type is specified, it's the most "default" floating-point type Rust has so feels like the best primitive type to have the documentation attached to.

(In summary, solving this can be left to a future PR.)

The last paragraph of the PR description was my attempt at a short summary. Here's a bigger one.

Without this part of the PR, removing the `mod tests {` wrapper module generates this error:
```
error[E0603]: constant import `MAX` is private
   --> core/tests/num/mod.rs:181:25

181 |         let num = u128::MAX as u128;
    |                         ^^^ private constant import
    |
note: the constant import `MAX` is defined here...

    |
1   | / macro_rules! uint_module {
2   | |     ($T:ident) => {
3   | |         use core::ops::{BitAnd, BitOr, BitXor, Not, Shl, Shr};
4   | |         use core::$T::*;
    | |             ^^^^^^^^^^^
...   |
316 | |     };
317 | | }
    | |_- in this expansion of `uint_module!`
    |
   ::: core/tests/num/u128.rs:1:1
    |
1   |   uint_module!(u128);
    |   ------------------ in this macro invocation
note: ...and refers to the constant `MAX` which is defined here
   --> /home/ben/rust/library/core/src/num/shells/int_macros.rs:44:9
    |
3   | / macro_rules! int_module {
4   | |     ($T:ident) => (int_module!($T, #[stable(feature = "rust1", since = "1.0.0")]););
5   | |     ($T:ident, #[$attr:meta]) => (
6   | |         #[doc = concat!(
...   |
44  | |         pub const MAX: $T = $T::MAX;
    | |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ you could import this directly
45  | |     )
46  | | }
    | |_- in this expansion of `int_module!`
    |
   ::: /home/ben/rust/library/core/src/num/shells/u128.rs:11:1
    |
11  |   int_module! { u128, #[stable(feature = "i128", since="1.26.0")] }
    |   ----------------------------------------------------------------- in this macro invocation
help: consider importing this constant instead
    |
181 |         let num = std::u128::MAX as u128;
```

Before this PR, name resolution must be concluding that `u128::MAX` cannot refer to the local `u128` module because it doesn't contain an item called `MAX`. But with the other changes in this PR the local `u128` module does contain an item `MAX` (which was previously at the path `u128::tests::MAX`)... except that the item is private. body:
I'm not sure a third macro makes sense. I think `addr_of!` should guarantee that if both the input and output types are raw pointers, then permissions are preserved and the behavior is identical to using `ptr::offset`. It's very useful for teaching if I can say that the only thing that matters for the permissions of raw pointers is where it originally comes from. Adding exceptions to that general rule is counterproductive.

In the same vein, the usual motivation for not roundtripping through `&T` is that doing so gives up permissions to write. The entire point of `addr_of!` is that it does not roundtrip through `&T`.

When doing `addr_of!(MY_STATIC)` you are creating the raw pointer, so it is consistent with the above rule that the resulting pointer is read-only. In this case, the `addr_of!` is where the raw pointer originally came from, so this decides its permissions.

body:
This *might* be a slight (unoptimized?) codegen regression, for things as simple as ([godbolt](https://godbolt.org/z/q8eejc7oo)):
```rust
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub fn r_next(mut r: std::ops::Range<usize>) -> Option<usize> {
    r.next()
}
```

Before:
```llvm
@alloc_3e1ebac14318b612ab4efabc52799932 = private unnamed_addr constant [186 x i8] c"unsafe precondition(s) violated: usize::unchecked_add cannot overflow\0A\0AThis indicates a bug in the program. This Undefined Behavior check is optional, and cannot be relied on for safety.", align 1

; <usize>::unchecked_add::precondition_check
define internal void @_RNvNvMs9_NtCs1p5UDGgVI4d_4core3numj13unchecked_add18precondition_checkCsb8r2Xq4BFYL_7example(i64 %lhs, i64 %rhs) unnamed_addr #0 {
; … (elided) …
bb1:                                              ; preds = %start
; call core::panicking::panic_nounwind
  call void @_ZN4core9panicking14panic_nounwind17h0c59dc9f7f043eadE(ptr align 1 @alloc_3e1ebac14318b612ab4efabc52799932, i64 186) #6
```
After:
```llvm
@alloc_3e1ebac14318b612ab4efabc52799932 = private unnamed_addr constant [186 x i8] c"unsafe precondition(s) violated: usize::unchecked_add cannot overflow\0A\0AThis indicates a bug in the program. This Undefined Behavior check is optional, and cannot be relied on for safety.", align 1
; … (elided) …

; <usize>::unchecked_add::precondition_check
; Function Attrs: inlinehint nounwind nonlazybind uwtable
define internal void @_RNvNvMs9_NtCs25W7cjsTkyH_4core3numj13unchecked_add18precondition_checkCsgRHkggJuglA_7example(i64 %lhs, i64 %rhs, ptr align 8 %0) unnamed_addr #0 {
; … (elided) …
bb1:                                              ; preds = %start
  %2 = getelementptr inbounds nuw { ptr, i64 }, ptr %_6, i64 0
  store ptr @alloc_3e1ebac14318b612ab4efabc52799932, ptr %2, align 8
; … (elided) …
; call core::panicking::panic_nounwind_fmt
  call void @_ZN4core9panicking18panic_nounwind_fmt17h42ee446b0f35d307E(ptr align 8 %_4, i1 zeroext false, ptr align 8 %0) #6
```

Notably, even if we ignore the extra IR needed to implement `fmt::Arguments::new_const`, the fact that `&[msg]` *is pointing to a stack array* (as opposed to e.g. `const { &[concat!(...)] }`) results in the constant string being stored on the stack *at runtime*.

(and unlike even `&[concat!(...)]`, the `let msg` blocks even *incidental* promotion)

---

That all aside, I am a bit surprised there isn't "just" a copy of `panic_nounwind` that has `#[track_caller]`, to avoid invoking `panic_nounwind_fmt` and have this extra codegen (assuming it matters at all, ofc, I just noticed this in passing for unrelated reasons).

body:
Also, the idea behind https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/127279 was probably incorrect after all.

If two syntax contexts have matching `(parent, outer_expn_id, outer_transparency)` tuples, they shouldn't just get identical (cloned) `SyntaxContextData`s, they should have the same `SyntaxContext` ids.

That's because all hygiene logic runs on comparing `SyntaxContext`, not `SyntaxContextData`s, so two different `SyntaxContexts` are considered different even if they datas are the same.
In other words, `SyntaxContextData` are assumed to be unique and interned (like `Symbol`s), and decoding should maintain this property.

body:
So, right now the logic in `target_features` that computes which `cfg(target-feature)` are set skips forbidden features, meaning they will never be set. However, cfg-check lists *all* known features, and thus doesn't warn about asking for these target features.

We will in the future have target features that are forbidden on some targets but can unstably be set on other targets. ("forbidden" doesn't mean they are never set, it means they cannot be changed -- but the target spec can still set them, so it could still make sense to query them.) One day we will likely have features that are stable on some targets but forbidden on others. It is not clear to me how this should be handled in cfg / cfg-check -- but what this PR does for now is change nothing about cfg, and cfg-check is just a lint so we can maybe figure out its non-trivial interactions with target features later, and until then it is okay that it does not complain about `cfg(target-feature = "soft-float")`.

body:
`expected` is obtained from `Parser`'s `expected_tokens` field. This list of expected tokens can be arbitrarily long depending on the size of the program because a token is added to the list every time the `check_*` functions are invoked inside the parser. 

But the actual expected keyword is located in the tail end of the list. For example, the parser adds the `where` keyword along with a few other tokens to the end of the expected tokens list after parsing a function's return type. 

So I arbitrarily chose the last ten tokens to make it efficient for the edit distance algorithm to process the entire list of keywords.

body:
> Is `lghi %r2` setting the return value here?

Yes, `lghi` on s390x is "Load Halfword Immediate". `%r2` register is the first return argument register on s390x when running a Linux-based system in Z-mode (see https://github.com/IBM/s390x-abi/releases/tag/v1.6.1, the addresses are 64-bit).

> (I can't read assembly code, I am afraid. I would have written this test differently but I guess the stuff above, with extern_func, tests whether "backchain" is passed to LLVM? So this test covers more than what I could have covered.)

The test is an assembly scanning test because different LLVM versions may interpret attributes differently. Scanning the resulting assembly is a more robust way to detect if the "backchain" option is passed down correctly.

The final type is not always guaranteed to be `Sized` (in the type system way), for example given

```rust
#![feature(trivial_bounds)]

}
```

the trait bound `Foo: Sized` will not hold, but attempting to compute the layout of `Foo` will error with `UnexpectedUnsized`.

@estebank What is the best way to suggest removing non contiguous empty lines. I.e.

```rust
1 /// Comment that should stay
2 
3 // More things that should stay
4 
5 struct X;
```

The `empty_lines()` functions returns the spans of lines `2` and `4` which should be removed, but their spans are `2:1-2:1` and `4:1-4:1`, so considered empty spans. `rustfix` has no problem applying this suggestion, while the `debug_assertion` causes the failure in CI. I wrote about this in the first commit message:

> The commit uses the name `'mir` everywhere for the lifetimes used with
`&Body` and `&MoveData`, replacing some other names: `'a`, `'flow`, and
`'cx`. I think this is a reasonable name because `'mir` is used for many

lifetime is shared between a `&Body` and a reference to something else,
the `'mir` lifetime name is so well-established that it's reasonable to
reuse it, rather than something non-specific like `'a`. (Naming
lifetimes is hard!)

I considered using `'a`, but one downside is if you have `Foo<'a, 'tcx>` and then you put a reference to that inside something else you get `&'b Foo<'a, 'tcx>`? Or maybe `&'a Foo<'b, 'tcx>`? And then if you put a reference to that inside something else again you get maybe `&'a Bar<'b, 'c, 'tcx>`?

body:
This PR's doing alot, and needs major rework, so I've only tried to review it at a high level, as I don't think the in-the-weeds stuff is worth it yet.

1. The changes to `ItemId` are intrusive to most of the rustdoc codebase, and not motivated at all. If these are nessessary, could that be explained, and send in a different, tighter-scoped, PR (that would be landed before this)
2. Making `Cache` be the only source of state for the `clean`->`json` lowering is quite a bad idea:
    - It requires adding a `TyCtxt`, which produces more changes to the rest of rustdoc.
    - It adds the interner field which isn't used for HTML, but is still present, which is unfortunate.
    - In present, it requires adding a `Lock`, but I don't think this is inherent.
3. There seem to be unrelated cleanups (like the removal of `FormatRenderer::cache`). These are should be merged into rustdoc, but not here! Again, the answer is a smaller, seperate PR, that just does one thing, and will be much easier to review.
author: aDotInTheVoid

body: Changing this is super-invasive. While it's possible that `Cache` should hold a `TyCtxt`, that should be changed in it's own PR (or at least commit), as it has implications for all of rustdoc, and should be discussed with the other maintainers. Doing it in the same commit makes this super-tricky to review.
author: aDotInTheVoid

body: Why are we using an `IndexSet`, instead of a `HashMap<ItemId, rustdoc_json_types::Id>` here? The latter seems far clearer (in my mind, at least).
author: aDotInTheVoid

body:
I don't think this is the right approach to threading some mutable state through the clean->JSON pass. For one, it hides the fact that `Cache` is mutable, why doesn't it take `&mut Cache`, so we can remove the `Lock` on the ItemId interning map.

But more broadly, I don't think we should be adding more things to `Cache` that are only needed here. I think a better aproach would be to do

```rust
// TODO: Better name for this
struct JsonItemConverter<'tcx> {
   tcx: TyCtxt<'tcx>,
   cache: Cache,
   id_interner: FxHashMap<ItemId, rustdoc_json_types::Id>
}
```

and then pass that to all the converting methods (either via a trait, or via methods on `impl JsonItemConverter`

body:
> rustdoc would start confusing things like a primitive & a module that documents its

But rustdoc doesn't do this today: [here's the docs for the module](https://stdrs.dev/nightly/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/std/prim_bool/index.html) and [and the primitive](https://stdrs.dev/nightly/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/std/primitive.bool.html)

>  a struct & a function with the same name, etc

Rustdoc also gets this right today. A [DefId](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_hir/def_id/struct.DefId.html) [uniquely indentifies a definiton](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/identifiers.html?highlight=DefId#in-the-hir), so the namespace it's in shouldn't be needed to disambiguate.

![](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4d2b1f12-207b-4117-9113-70e02707b98a)

See https://godbolt.org/z/KPc3Kav4q for how the HIR gets created here, and notice how both `foo`s have different DefId's.

---

In general, by the time we get to Hir and DefId's we shouldn't need to be worryied about what namespace an item exists in, as that's all handled in name-resolution. Was there a concrete reason why this needed to be added, or did you believe it was necessary (which is totally fine, I'm just trying to understand if there's something I'm missing)?
author: aDotInTheVoid

body: You can just use the `.len()` for this (which is what [`IndexMap`](https://github.com/indexmap-rs/indexmap/blob/abdd155f73331040991f24eaff6f37976097711e/src/map/core/raw.rs#L70) does internally). Yes this means we need to implement a bit more logic in rustdoc, but it make the nature as a Map clearer (rather than being a set), and means you don't have to pay the overhead of `IndexMap` (vs hashbrown's HashMap)

It's sound if you don't touch it in _any_ way after running `Box`'s drop I think (i.e. not even move). But generally yes.

body:
Writing `uninit()` into  `self.element` will likely be elided in release mode, but explicitly writing `uninit()` into `self.element` would let sanitizers (e.g. Miri) explicitly catch if the field is later read as initialized, even if `T: Copy`.

body:
So this turned out to be non-trivial, because there is currently no way to distinguish
```rust
let x: T = y;
```
from
```rust
let x = y as T
```
by looking at the MIR alone (without relying on the exact order of MIR statements).

So our options here are
* Leave the diagnostic as is, calling some coercion casts just "coercions" (technically correct).
* Revert the wording and call all coercions "casts" (technically wrong).
* Add some additional diagnostic-only information into the MIR to allow us to distinguish them and output the optimal diagnostic (which is really just one word). This is currently unprecedented as far as I'm aware.

I'm unsure what the best option here is and would appreciate your input :)
author: lukas-code

body:
I would prefer the third option, i.e. to add some diagnostic only info. That being said I think you should check with people who work on MIR more (miri or miropt zulip streams maybe?).

The first option (using "coercion" when the user wrote a cast) could be OK. If you want we can leave the third option as a follow up (please try to do it though 😄).

I'm not sure what's the best way to phrase this, but I don't think "unsound" is right here. 

The drive on its own *is* sound. It's the combination with `ManuallyDrop::drop` which is unsound. And since the latter is unsafe, it falls into its safety requirements that the `ManuallyDrop` value is not used after the call. 

That being said, basically all intended usages of `ManuallyDrop` do not combine with derived traits (since the user of the type can always call them after the value is dropped), so this is an important foot gun to highlight. I just feel like there is a better way to explain it maybe.

body:
I think documentation should clarify that this also applies to any types that directly contain `Box<_>`, like `(Box<T>, u8)` or `struct Foo(Box<T>);`.

I also believe that per current rules, calling `ManuallyDrop::drop()` on any type that directly contains `Box<_>` is insta-UB, even if you don’t move it afterwards. Technically, it doesn’t neccessarily count as producing an invalid value:

> “Producing” a value happens any time a value is assigned to or read from a place, passed to a function/primitive operation or returned from a function/primitive operation.

but at least touching it in any way (like creating a reference) is certainly UB.
author: GoldsteinE

body: If you don't name the place after calling `ManuallyDrop::drop`, everything is fine; the place isn't touched after that point. Because `ManuallyDrop` does not have any drop glue, it does not get a `drop_in_place` terminator at the end of scope, and thus the place is never "used" implicitly by the language, and no reference is created unless you create it yourself.
author: CAD97

body:
I have reworded the text to clarify that the UB also applies to types containing `Box`.

I am pretty sure that calling `ManuallyDrop::drop()` on a type containing `Box` is *not* UB. https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines/issues/245 only states that using the `ManuallyDrop` later is UB. If you believe that `ManuallyDrop::drop()` is insta-UB, then I would like a citation to prove otherwise.

Of note, Miri doesn't seem to complain anything if I create a reference to an already-dropped `ManuallyDrop<Box<T>>`. I believe this is because we are still undecided on whether the existence of a `&T` implies that the `T` must be valid.

body:
I think there're two orthogonal things here:
1. Effect on ABI
2. Effect on performance

For (1), it places constraints on "C" ABI only, and should not effect Rust ABI. For (2), Rust compiler, with its freedom on `extern "Rust"`, can freely apply inreg to functions. These are completely orthogonal, it's perfectly fine to enable (2) without (1).

For this reason, I think this PR should focus on (1). The option name probably should also be renamed to reflect that. Maybe `-Zc-abi-reg-param`? (2) is an performance improvement and can be made at any time -- arguably we can just make it a default for all `extern "Rust"` functions on x86 if perf run is positive.

> In this case cargo could provide a user friendly way using only a single command or flag which would set all the required rustdoc flags. Still there would be full control over all flags on the rustdoc level.

If this feature were being added in a vacuum, I might agree. But we already have a ton of cases where it's Rustc, not Cargo, that takes care of deciding all the cfg options (except `feature=`, of course).

For example, `rustc --test` sets cfg(test), `rustc --target` sets the target cfgs, `rustdoc` sets cfg(doc), and `rustdoc --test` sets cfg(doctest). The tool itself makes these decisions, not Cargo.

Default CPU to pass to LLVM. Corresponds to llc -mcpu=$cpu. Defaults to “generic”.

> features: [Cow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html)<'static, [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>
Default target features to pass to LLVM. These features overwrite -Ctarget-cpu but can be overwritten with -Ctarget-features. Corresponds to llc -mattr=$features. Note that these are LLVM feature names, not Rust feature names!

Codegen fully identifies a vtable using just the `Option<ty::PolyExistentialTraitRef<'tcx>>`:

So how can it be that Miri would require more than this? Is it just that currently it happens to be the case that vtables only depend on the principal (i.e., never depend on projections or auto traits) but we want to reserve the right to change this later?
author: RalfJung

body: "allocated" sounds odd here. IMO the previous distinction makes more sense -- the "expected" info comes from the type, and that is compared with the actual info stored in the vtable pointer. There is no "expected vtable", there's just an expected list of predicates. IOW, `List<ty::PolyExistentialPredicate<'tcx>>` isn't a vtable, only `GlobalAlloc::Vtable` is a vtable.
author: RalfJung

body: There's a very detailed comment at the top of this file explaining what it is for.
author: RalfJung

body: Please don't call this a "vtable". This is confusing the "information required to compute a vtable" with the resulting output, the vtable.
author: RalfJung

body:
Codegen fully identifies a vtable using a `Option<PolyExistentialTraitRef>` *and* a self `Ty`.

Miri doesn't require the full set of predicates, either, technically, but computing the set of projections that correspond to a vtable requires also using the self type to compute what the projections would be. We could also pass that in to the validity, since it's stored in the allocation, but that would be pretty expensive to test a bunch of projection goals every time we want to validate vtable equality.

body:
Fundamentally, I think what happens here is that we have two forms of normalization here (type system normalization reducing e.g. associated const paths, and const eval normalization evaluating a fully "type system normalized" const path to its value). The type system grabbed the term "normalize" as if it was the only kid in town, so now we have to figure out what terminology other systems can use.

These things used to be called `eval`, but that is quite confusing because a function with that name should return a *value*, and that's not what these functions return. They return the same type as their argument. So in standard PL terms, this is more "normalization" than "evaluation".
author: RalfJung

body: That sounds very odd to me. The fundamental thing we can do with a (fully monomorphized) type system constant is get its valtree. This needs *evaluation* as it has to run the code that defines this constant. A bunch of other systems need that, e.g. the interpreter when a const generic argument is used as a value in the function body. Why should we not have such an operation and how else should other parts of the compiler get the valtree?
author: RalfJung

body:
fwiw its not *just* a naming issue- if we were to try and update the `eval_x` methods to be the kind of normalization that the type system requires then we would have to return the nested goals of the normalization to the caller which in the past has caused soundness bugs.

That is the most significant motivation for this refactor- it makes it much more likely that const generics doesn't have subtle bugs around normalization of const aliases. Though I do also think having `ty::Const` have symmetry with `ty::Ty` is much nicer than having symmetry with `mir::Const` as it makes working with consts similar to working with types and generally I've found that where there's divergence in logic between type system consts and types, there tends to be bugs.

One caveat we noticed — which is really a separate concern — is that there's no way to specify eabihf with no FP. That sounds nonsensical, but it's potentially useful with integer MVE, which uses the same registers. Clang [achieves that with `+nofp`](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/55d51dd9dca8220ffaf9260d56dae9f5c34b7120/clang/lib/Driver/ToolChains/Arch/ARM.cpp#L701), which seems to get [translated into `-mfpu=none`](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/55d51dd9dca8220ffaf9260d56dae9f5c34b7120/clang/lib/Driver/ToolChain.cpp#L259), but I can't find a way to control that through Rust.

My understanding [from the zulip conversation](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/187780-t-compiler.2Fllvm/topic/nocapture.20and.20allocation.20elimination/near/523896671) is that since the allocation ends there's nothing further that the callee could do that would be relevant to aliasing rules of this allocation.

Whether or not the allocator touches the memory afterwards (e.g. for zeroing), isn't relevant to this side of the allocator boundary.

I assume we need to tell LLVMs both things separately because they just happen to be tracked separately.

body:
For sanity, let $R$ = `ty.references_error()` and $C$ = `ty.contains_error()`. $R$ checks if `ty` has `TypeFlags::HAS_ERROR`, while $C$ checks each contained type for being a `TyKind::Error`. 

I'm not knowledgeable enough about deeper usage of `TypeFlags` to clarify why, but $C$ seems to result in similar output to `R && ty.to_string().contains("{type error}")`. 

(I think `Ty`'s inner `GlobalCtxt` lets `FlagComputation::for_kind(...)` attribute errors to `ty` during `CtxtInterners::intern_ty(...)`, even if it's not about what `ty` directly contains.)

Anyways, when just using $R$, many tests fail as they're missing expected diagnostics. For example, `tests/ui/const-generics/issues/issue-56445-1.rs` fails with this:

```rust
--- not found errors (from test file) ---
ERROR     line   9: `&str` is forbidden as the type of a const generic parameter
```

It feels like $R$ is (loosely) a superset of $C$. Creating $C$ results in the appropriate output for this check.

Ah well, slight issue here. Because rust-analyzer doesn't support something like `invocationStrategy` for rustfmt, it needs an absolute path to be provided here otherwise it'll look for the closest Cargo.toml and try to call e.g. `src/bootstrap/build/host/rustfmt/bin/rustfmt` which obviously does not exist.

The vscode config gets around this by sticking `${workspaceFolder}` in the string but that doesn't work here because it's a vscode thing. I tried getting around it with this concat trick, which does make rustfmt work, but then other parts of LSP choke on the input while trying to parse it because Emacs is not expecting there to be any functions getting called in this file. Not great.

The optimal solution would be to fix rust-analyzer at some point, what workaround should we go with for now? The easiest one would be to leave a note about how the user needs to adjust the path by hand. We could automate it as well where we just fix the path in setup.rs before the file is written to its proper location, but then that'll break the hash-based versioning because now what's actually used would always be different from the template.

body:
I think we should move `from_anon_const` and `try_from_lit` to `hir_ty_lowering` too since they are also lowerings from hir to `ty::`. Looking  through uses of `from_anon_const` I guess this is not super trivial, though I think should be doable. afaict there are two callers:

WF checking of type definitions lowers an enum discriminant to a `ty::Const` in order to require it to be evaluatable through the type system (`wfcheck.rs` line 1186). This should be relatively easy to remove as I don't think we should even be creating a `ty::Const` in the first place. It should suffice to just create a [`mir::consts::UnevaluatedConst`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/mir/consts/struct.UnevaluatedConst.html) and then call [`tcx.const_eval_poly`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/ty/context/struct.TyCtxt.html#method.const_eval_poly) and look at the returned value to see whether the discriminant was evaluated successfully or not.

The other case being `const_evaluatable_predicates_of` which seems a bit more annoying. It's only used by `feature(generic_const_exprs)` to look at all the anon consts in an item signature and synthesize where clauses that the anon const can be evaluated without error. The way we do this currently is by walking the hir and finding any hir anon consts then lowering them to a `ty::Const`.

I think it should be possible to instead change `const_evaluatable_predicates_of` to instead visit the lowered forms of signatures and directly look for `ty::ConstKind::Unevaluated` instead. That'd look something like accepting the WIP set of `ty::Predicates` as an argument to the function and visiting those, then matching on the `def_id` to see if we should call `fn_sig` or `type_of` or look at struct fields etc for additional places there could be anon consts.

Can talk more about this 1:1 if you'd like since I think it's pretty likely that the `const_evaluatable_predicates_of` explanation is not very good :3

The whole story of consts in rustdoc is a mess (see #83035). The TLDR is that we use both `hir::Const` and `ty::Const` and we basically need to use both. It's an open question whether/in which cases rustdoc should show the original const expression (`hir`) or the evaluated/evaluatable version (`ty`). There's advantages to both. So in the middle of processing some `hir` nodes, rustdoc may need to lower a hir const to a ty const. I don't think we'll be able to get rid of that anytime soon.

You're right that clippy doesn't need it though; I think it did when I originally wrote this code but was since modified to no longer need it.

body:
I would recommend caution with this approach, since it is inherently racey. For example, it assumes that it can close the handle before `rustc` is able to print. There can also be assumptions here about `PIPE_BUF` and other pipe behaviors. This can be unreliable on some systems. For example, on macOS, this should fail occasionally. 

That's why cargo's tests which exercise this same behavior use a proc-macro to synchronize with `rustc`. (see [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/a06986cda652fb9d91ce027977d2126efa111e4f/tests/testsuite/build.rs#L6576-L6776)). That way the test can ensure that the handle is closed *before* `rustc` prints. Those tests also have some comments about the hazards of how this works.

body:
If the regular expression engine used by FileCheck supports lookahead, I can write:

```
// CHECK-NOT: {{call (?!void @llvm\.assume)}}
```

But it doesn’t, so I have to use a more complex regular expression. The idea is:

```
   (?!d) =>                          [^d]|$
  (?!cd) =>   c(?!d)|[^c]|$ =>     c([^d]|$)|[^c]|$
 (?!bcd) =>  b(?!cd)|[^b]|$ =>   b(c([^d]|$)|[^c]|$)|[^b]|$
(?!abcd) => a(?!bcd)|[^a]|$ => a(b(c([^d]|$)|[^c]|$)|[^b]|$)|[^a]|$
```

So `(?!void @llvm\.assume)` becomes that complex regular expression.

body:
The reason that this is the case is because every other feature got incrementally carved out of `const_maybe_uninit_assume_init` and stabilized under new names, and people okayed it instead of pausing to reconsider how the feature was divided.

By renaming and then stabilizing a feature name that didn't previously exist, we make the history notably harder to understand, because then that becomes a feature that never had an issue open for it.

So no. We should not. The appropriate time to fuss over the name was every single other stabilization ago.

body:
IMO we make the history less confusing by picking feature names that reflect what is actually covered by the feature. :shrug: 


it is also unclear to me in which sense this makes history "harder to understand" -- we remove the tracking issue number upon stabilization, so clearly there's no expectation of tracking history that way. And `git blame` will work just fine either way.

If you are thinking of people searching for the feature name in the issue tracker, it would be trivial to edit the tracking issue to also mention the split-off feature gates, and if that is something people care about it should have been done as part of the previous PR that stabilized parts of this feature. Furthermore, to my knowledge we don't have a standard or expectation about feature names along the lines of what you are saying here, so it seems futile to try to partially enforce it. In fact we often partially stabilize a feature, and then the tracking issue gets updated to remove what has been stabilized so that it is clear what is still tracked here -- yes that is confusing, but it seems to be standard procedure. The tracking issue always only reflects the status quo, it doesn't necessarily explain the past that got us here.

It seems to me you're making up a new standard here and now trying to unilaterally enforce it.

body:
@rust-lang/lang this PR marks three intrinsics as const-callable from stable const fn: `likely`, `unlikely`, and `ub_checks`. They were already exposed on stable before through a loophole in our recursive const stability checks (specifically, via `#[allow_internal_unstable]`), so this doesn't expose anything new -- it just acknowledges what is already real.

Not sure if you want to FCP this, given that the actual exposure on stable happened a while ago. If you do want to (retroactively) FCP this I would suggest to do that asynchronously, in a separate issue -- I don't think it has to block this PR, since this PR doesn't actually change anything about what is exposed on stable.
author: RalfJung

body:
I changed this to `raw` since we want to show all `const fn` as `const fn`, no matter their const stability attributes. A `const fn` that's unstable should get the "const: unstable" marker, but it should still show as `const fn`.

The intent probably already was to show `const fn` even for unstable const fn, hence the `is_unstable_const_fn`, but this does *not* show it for `const fn` that have `#[unstable]` and no const stability attributes -- but those functions *are* callable via their `#[unstable]` feature gate.

So let's just use `is_const_fn_raw` which easily does the right thing.
author: RalfJung

body:
@oli-obk FYI this renames `is_const_fn_raw` to `is_const_fn`, and replaces the previous `is_const_fn` by `is_stable_const_fn` which doesn't quite have the same semantics but close enough for the one (!) user in rustc that actually wants to use this.

A bunch of other places used `is_const_fn` when they shouldn't have -- in particular, [this one](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/d6f247f3d52f529e7145eb355ac9660a49d0d8c9/compiler/rustc_passes/src/reachable.rs#L47) is scary. Surely whether we consider something reachable should not depend on which feature gates are enabled in the current crate... Also, [this one](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/ab8673501ce13573c06b5989b179f5cfed85c771/compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/check_undefined_transmutes.rs#L42) is supposed to lint in all const fn we declared, not just the ones for which we have the feature gate on.

body:
I was just randomly looking at this patch and found a potential issue.

Don't you have a race here?
What if the Future is polled right now?
We already took the waker which was still the noop when we cloned it and released the Mutex on the waker.
Now the Future sets the waker and then check again that it is not finished. But we as we haven't decremented the ref-count yet (we do that only in the next line) so the Future will return Pending and nobody is ever going to wake it.

Since you are using a Mutex for the synchronization of the Waker, I suggest to also use this lock to communicate to the future that we are finished and that the result can be taken out even if the ref-count is still 2.

body:
> by using raw pointers which for some reason we don't lint on.

We don't lint against raw pointers because that's often what we're trying to push people toward (among other options).  We lint against references because it's easier to get that wrong without realizing.  E.g., it's fine to have aliasing pointers to some data as long as you're careful to not race the accesses, but it's never fine to have aliasing live mutable references.  But taking potentially long-lived references to mutable statics makes it really easy to do that accidentally.

To make this particular case safer, I'd probably move `STACK_TRACE` into that `let stack = unsafe { .. }` block.  Then it can't be directly accessed later while the reference to it via that slice is live, which is the main danger.

Probably I'd also expect this function to be `unsafe extern "C" fn ..` since there's a safety requirement here that must be upheld by callers (the function is not reentrant).  Not sure if there's some practical reason preventing that here.

Assuming that safety invariant is upheld, the use of `static mut` here, as revised, seems fine to me in the context of what we were trying to achieve as a lang matter.  This is plausibly the kind of use case that argues against deprecating `static mut` entirely (see #53639).

body:
Whether a result is a false positive or a true positive (or a false negative or a true negative) depends on what you want fn pointer comparison to do.
* If you want to compare the address the function pointer corresponds to, there should be no false (incorrect) results (positive or negative) IIUC.
* If you want to see if two fn pointers correspond to the same function, there may be false positives (fn pointers you got from different functions comparing equal) and false negatives (fn pointers you got from the same function comparing inequal).

Given the above context describing the second viewpoint, I think "false positives and false negatives" is correct here.

body:
> I see. Then that code would have to assume that the Rust runtime is not online yet, since it's part of the boot vector table. Do we expect this to be normally done? I'm not sure how easy it is to program these sorts of details for VEX specifically.

I'm not sure if this is particularly relevant to allocation locks, but the Rust runtime is not part of the boot vector table on this target.

Just to clarify a bit about user program startup - VEXos sets up the "userspace" (a block of memory starting at `0x03800000`) and begins executing instructions at `0x03800020`. No interrupt vectors or any kind of real "boot code" is needed, as the user processor is already fully setup (with FPU enabled, interrupts configured, timers setup, etc...) before any Rust code is executed. All that VEXos needs as an entrypoint is some instructions at `0x03800020` which in our case is some `global_asm` we toss into our linkerscript's `.boot` section that just loads the stack pointer before branching into actual Rust code.

The only time Rust code would interact with interrupts is if the user explicitly decided to overwrite VEXos's [VBAR](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0601/latest/AArch32-Registers/VBAR--Vector-Base-Address-Register) with their own vector table, which would break a lot of OS-internal things such as timers and the user CPU's scheduler if steps weren't taken to call back to the OS's own interrupt handlers in the new vector table (VEXos does provide hooks into its own interrupt handlers for this specific case, mainly for FreeRTOS ports). I don't think wrapping allocation in a critical section is a bad idea here, but it's important to know that hooking any sort of interrupts or masking interrupts for an extended period of time requires cooperation with OS internals in a way that's different from a typical bare-metal system.

body:
> Given that almost every PR changes compiler or library, and that those are already in the files-to-track -- is this really worth it? 

I haven't checked the exact numbers but we get fair amount of PRs that don’t touch the `compiler` or `library`. Each of those cuts the PR CI time for `x86_64-gnu-tools` in half and the same applies for a lot of runners in merge CI (if the PR isn’t rolled up with others that touch `compiler` or `library`). > In general this shows that download-rustc=if-unchanged is very tricky to get right -- the rustc build has a ton of inputs, bootstrap assembles various environment variables, etc. This list will inevitably get out of date as some logic somewhere changes.

I might recommend rephrasing/reorganizing this section along the lines of:

1. What is Emscripten and how this target integrates? (e.g. Emscripten is a C/C++ toolchain not related to Rust used for running C/C++ code on the web)
2. Why Emscripten is used and how Rust integrates. (e.g. Emscripten implements POSIX in terms of web APIs and provides a C standard library for that)
3. How this contrasts to other wasm targets in Rust (e.g. unlike `wasm32-unknown-unknown` it can run C/C++ and provides a full implementation of libc/libstd, unlike `wasm32-wasip1` it requires JS glue code to run on the web because the interface between wasm/JS isn't standard)

In terms of C/C++ I'd recommend focusing on both that and library support for Emscripten. Emscripten isn't just about C/C++ but also all the polyfills provided for libraries like SDL (IIRC). The contrast to `wasm32-unknown-unknown` can indicate that the unknown target has no support for C/C++ or anything that requires JS (or at least not inherently).

When comparing to `wasm32-wasip1` I'd recommend mostly contrasting it in terms of web support. The WASI target has no standard way of accessing web APIs where Emscripten has the ability to run arbitrary JS from wasm and access many web APIs. In the end the difference here will likely boil down to "are you running on the web or not" but that doesn't alone accurately capture the nuance of you can run WASI on the web but you just won't have access to the full suite of web APIs by default.

---

That may be more words than desired, sorry about that! Overall I think the wording is fine as-is, so what I'm thinking here is just minor updates here and there. Feel free to take or leave any suggestions as you see fit!

This does not build from source. emsdk is just an installer for the toolchain.

Interestingly, [the code for the emscripten compiler toolchain](https://github.com/emscripten-core/emscripten/) itself has no compilation step, it is implemented in a mixture of Python and JavaScript. So you can just modify the source files in place and immediately have a patched compiler. The standard library / sysroot is compiled as needed (since `emcc` implements many many different ABIs it doesn't make sense to ship prebuilt static libraries, it builds them as needed and caches them).

All of the compiled code needed for implementing the compiler (as opposed to host wasm code) is upstream either in [binaryen](https://github.com/WebAssembly/binaryen) or in llvm itself.

I think we should remove this. It came from a comment in `wasm32-unknown-unknown` that most tests don't work there, but most tests do work in Emscripten. Also, `wasm32-unknown-unknown` sort of feels like a default wasm target, but it's very limited. 

Most people will want one of:
* wasm32-unknown + wasm-bindgen: convenient way to write rust projects specifically targeting web that don't need any C/C++.
* emscripten: make an existing rust project work in web with minimal changes to the code at the cost of bigger code size. Can also be run as a CLI with node.
* wasi: Make lightweight sandboxed cli applications (can be used as a lighter weight replacement for containers). Don't need a JavaScript runtime. Resulting binaries can also be run on the web. When targeting the web, has a larger code size than wasm-bindgen, can be larger or smaller than Emscripten depending. Requires more porting work than Emscripten, but less than wasm-bindgen. Fewer features than Emscripten. Compared to wasm-bindgen it has no js interop but in trade the standard library works.

In most cases, people really need a specific one of these targets. They are not very interchangeable, but it makes sense for `wasm32-unknown` to direct people to wasi if they are looking to test webassembly support "in general".

author: RalfJung

body:
> Why will FUTEX_LOCK_PI always succeed?

Yes, `FUTEX_LOCK_PI` always succeeds.

For `FUTEX_WAIT` in the original test:
- If it is contended, `FUTEX == HELD`, syscall put the waiter thread into sleep.
- If it is not, `FUTEX == FREE != HELD`, syscall fails immediately.

`FUTEX_WAIT`/`FUTEX_WAKE` do not perform state changes of `FUTEX`; all state changes are performed in user space.

For `FUTEX_LOCK_PI` in this test:
- If it is contended, syscall changes `FUTEX` from the owner thread's `tid` to `tid | FUTEX_WAITERS` (this is tested in the `loop` below), and put the waiter thread into sleep.
- If it is not, `FUTEX == 0`, syscall changes `FUTEX` from `0` to the new owner's `tid`, and returns immediately.

So all state changes are done in the kernel. `FUTEX_LOCK_PI` always succeeds.

body:
I reviewed the implementation of PI futexes in the kernel. It seems to be using a fair unlock protocol where, on unlock, ownership of the mutex is passed directly to the next waiting thread.

While fair unlocking has theoretical benefits, in practice it tends to be much slower than unfair locking which leaves the mutex in an unlocked state and just wakes up a waiter. The reason is that waking up a thread has a long latency but it's very common for a single thread to repeatedly lock and unlock the same mutex. If lock ownership is forcibly transferred to a waiting thread then this prevents any other thread from acquiring the mutex until that thread wakes up.

As such, I don't think PI futexes are suitable for use as the default mutex implementation for Rust. They should be provided in a crate for specialized use cases where PI is needed and the performance cost of fair unlocking is acceptable.

> ‹vector_arg›: A vector_arg has one of the following types:

> - A float or _Decimal32.
> - A double or _Decimal64.
> - A structure equivalent to one of the above. A structure is equivalent to a type 𝑇 if and *only if it has exactly one member, which is either of type 𝑇 itself or a structure equivalent to type 𝑇*.

Looking at the existing code, is the handling of ZST platform dependent? (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/125854)

author: taiki-e

body:
This is unfortunately a bit more complicated due to historical reasons.   For the purposes of deciding whether an aggregate is a "structure equivalent to a float or vector", zero-sized members *in C* are *not* ignored.  The presence of a zero-sized bitfield, nested struct, or nested array member does make the aggregate *not equivalent*, i.e. it will be passed in GPRs and not in FPRs/VRs.

However, for C++ types, there are some zero-sized members that *are* ignored; this applies in particular to zero-sized base classes as well as C++20 empty data members (marked with `[[no_unique_address]]`).  This is not currently documented in the ABI (but then again, the ABI doesn't document anything about C++ ...).

The question is, what does this now mean for Rust?   My understanding is that Rust here attempts to be ABI-compatible with *C* only (not C++), and therefore I think it makes sense that Rust should be treated like C, i.e. zero-sized members are not ignored.  Current Rust code seems to correctly implement this for FP types via `is_single_fp_element`, so I think this PR should do the same for vector types.

As to the second question, what if the whole argument is zero-sized?  Both the strict reading of the ABI document and the actual GCC/clang implementation agree that this is passed via implicit pointer (which arguably doesn't make much sense, but we cannot change this anymore).  So the current Rust code looks correct to me.

body: This can throw away quite a bit of generated data, depending on the granularity of `fill_bytes` calls. When generating a `u32` via its `Random` impl, it generates one block of 64 bytes and throws away 60 of them. That's terrible for performance no matter how much SIMD you throw at it. It's better to keep a buffer of one or several blocks, incrementally consume the buffered bytes, and only refill once they're all used up. The logic for that is slightly more fiddly but it's absolutely worth it. That's another "performance optimization" that needs to be done before stabilization because it changes observable behavior.

body:
Most 32- and 64-bit architectures don't have native 8-bit registers or operations on them. Even when they do (x86's vestigial `al`, `bl`, `cl`, etc.), they're never *cheaper* than natively supported widths in any way that would be applicable here (e.g., if you operate on a lot of values at once, smaller types are nice for SIMD, but here we only have one counter). The best you can hope for is that the sign/zero extensions and truncations can be mostly optimized out and don't cost anything extra on loads/stores, which is often but not always the case.

The only exception are some odd "8 bit ALU with 16 bit address space" architectures of which only AVR has any semblance of Rust support.

The problem is this line, PR CI runs compiletest tool tests at `--stage 0`, which uses a prebuilt beta rustc. This beta rustc does not know about `avr-unknown-unknown` because it doesn't exist to beta rustc, it only knows about `avr-unknown-gnu-atmega328`. You need to guard this with something like

```rs
#[cfg(bootstrap)]
("avr-unknown-gnu-atmega328", false),
#[cfg(not(bootstrap))]
("avr-unknown-unknown", false),
```

Then T-release should delete the `#[cfg(bootstrap)]`'d `avr-unknown-gnu-atmega328` next bump and when a beta rustc knowns about the renamed `avr-unknown-unknown` target delete `#[cfg(not(bootstrap))]` attribute.

IIUC, a variant corresponds to a niche. I convert to a discriminant(`variant_idx`) to a niche by `(d - niche_variants.start).wrapping_add(niche_start)`, so this returns an iterator for all niches.

Then we pass a niche as a pointer, the max alignment of a niche is `max_for_offset(niche)`. For example:
- the max alignment of `8` is `8`

- the max alignment of `26`(`0b11010`) is `2`

Well, so the param-env of this `ValuePairs` is *conceptually* distinct from param-env of the `TypeError` that may be emitted, since (well, in the future perhaps) the `TypeError` may have instantiated binders in scope as well.

So like, imagine a type error between[^a] `for<T: Foo<Assoc = i32>> fn(<T as Foo>::Assoc)` and `fn(u32)`. Why is it correct at all as part of a conditional expression like a `while` or `if`? It only takes on its magic "until the end of the string" meaning when used as an argument to `std::string`'s functions, doesn't it? Which the control-flow expressions are not invocations of.

https://cplusplus.com/reference/string/string/find/

> Return Value
> The position of the first character of the first match.
> If no matches were found, the function returns [string::npos](https://cplusplus.com/string::npos).

`npos` isn't magic, it's in practice just a way to say `-1`. find() returns npos if something isn't found, and at that point we don't take this if / exit the loop.

Like, the problem inheres in the fact that we have "sanity checks" to begin with.

First, I've read that code. I can't call it sane with a straight face.

Second, the entire purpose of a "sanity check" is to attempt to do post-hoc checking of layout invariants, after we've created these invalid layouts. We _do_ have something for that, but it's called a `#[test]`.
author: workingjubilee

body:
> Yes, but we already "return" an ICE based on `cfg!(debug_assertions)`

Yeah that's how debug asserts work? If `debug_assertions` are enabled they sometimes "return" a panic rather than the wrong thing, but here you're making it so that if `debug_assertions` are enabled, we're suddenly starting to return the correct thing instead, which seems confusing to me.

> Like, the problem inheres in the fact that we have "sanity checks" to begin with.

I don't see the problem with sanity checks here or the advantage of moving this code to a `#[test]`. When the sanity check is enabled (by enabling debug assertions) it's like we're running the test for every layout that's computed by the compiler and that's how we're finding the bugs like the one you're fixing here in the first place. If we just `#[test]` some list of predefined layouts, then we would have never found this bug.

body:
Sounds plausible, but if we're going that route, then we should really make sure that upcast unsizing coercions and ptr-to-ptr casts behave consistently, so we don't up in this situation:
```rust
let ptr: *const (dyn Trait + Send) = /* ... */;

let ptr2: *const dyn Send = ptr as *const dyn Send; // unsizing coercion, changes vtable as if we unsized the original type to `dyn Send` directly
let _: *const (dyn Trait + Send) = transmute(ptr2); // UB!!, vtable doesn't match

let ptr2: *const W<dyn Send> = ptr as *const W<dyn Send>; // ptr-to-ptr cast, leaves vtable
let _: *const (dyn Trait + Send) = transmute(ptr2); // fine, vtable matches
```
author: lukas-code

body:

But also, the upcast coercions don't change the vtable either.

body:
I guess I'll just change the way we do const stability enforcement on top of this. I'd still like to see three things fixed in this PR:

1. Rework all of that logic starting with `// Check that all trait bounds that are marked as ~const can be satisfied.` -- it's no longer true and no longer doing anything, since `~const` bounds are not even *in* the `predicates_of` anymore. Ideally we'd adjust that logic to register and check `const_conditions` for all conditionally const items, and keep that as a **failsafe** for making sure we don't accidentally forget to check `~const` bounds in HIR, given that many different HIR operations can translate into call terminators during MIR lowering. That's what I meant by (1.) above, not that HIR typeck shouldn't be primarily responsible for enforcing constness.
1. Remove that call to `Instance::try_resolve` call, since it's really not conceptually well-founded; we shouldn't be *specializing* constness checking to specific impl items, since this is both inconsistent and unnecessary IMO, and easily side-stepped with things like trivial where clause and indirection via generics.
1. It would be very nice if you tried to despaghettify the existing logic. There's a lot of nesting of thes `if` statements and I'm not totally certain that it should exist. @ralfjung had an idea, and this is kinda what I mean by (2.) above, but ideally we'd uplift the const enforcement of trait methods to a new `NonConstOp` implementation and enforce const trait calls via that (i.e. override its `status` with `Status::Unstable(sym::const_traits)`). I'm not sure why we even need to care about the `effects` feature gate in MIR checking, since IMO that should (at least for now, obviously being removed later) gate *just* the enforcement of effects in HIR typeck -- MIR should enforce these unconditionally.

body:
While reviewing this I've written down the desired behavior of `trait_has_impl_which_may_shadow_dyn` myself to make sure I don't just accept the impl as is. This may be helpful as a slightly different perspective on what we're doing here:

We only disable the builtin impls for traits with associated types, as only these may have unsound overlap. We correctly handle overlapping methods by always using the builtin impl for them, necessary for `<dyn Any as Any>::type_id`.

For such traits

- there exists an impl which does not require `Sized` on a non-rigid self-type
- unless this impl has a where-bound on the self-type which requires the self-type to implement a trait which is known to not hold:

the trait may hold if it is not `Sized` and
- it is an auto-trait, or
- the trait is a builtin trait implemented for `dyn Trait (+ Auto)*`, or
- the trait is part of the elaborated predicates list, i.e. a super-trait, or
- there exists an user-written impl which applies to this trait object
    - either implemented directly for `dyn Trait (+ Auto)*`
    - blanket impl
        - unless this impl has a where-bound on the self-type which requires the self-type to implement a trait which is known to not hold -> recurse
        - or the self-type is an alias whose item bounds cannot apply -> recurse

body:
>we may also want to emit a warn by default lint for all impls which disable the builtin object impl 🤔 even if that lint will mostly be unactionable 😅 potentially even regardless of whether we actually disable the impl because the trait has an associated type as adding such an impl will mean that adding an associated type will cause your trait to not be object safe anymore which is likely surprising

I'm really curious of the fallout of this is (i.e. how widespread is this pattern). There are effectively four levels of strictness here:
1) Error on all impls that may overlap with the builtin impl, regardless of it they have an associated type
2) Error on all impls that may overlap with the builtin impl and have an associated type, whether or not that associated type can overlap the builtin associated type
3) Error on all impls that may overlap with the builtin impl and have an associated type that *can* overlap with the builtin associated type
4) Error on all impls that may overlap with the builtin impl and have an associated type that *does* overlap with the builtin associated type.

I'm not sure if there's a meaningful difference between 3 and 4, but there may be in what we can *prove*.

I imagine 1 and 2 are probably non-starters in terms of breakage, but 3 or 4 may be worth doing at the coherence level. This is instead of the PR as-is, which *allows* overlapping impls but *disables* the builtin impl.

Of course, 3 and 4 get harder to implement when you consider GATs (which aren't yet dyn compatible but will be), but maybe not unapproachably harder.

I think this PR is compatible with later switching to one of the 4 sets of rules above, since those are I think more strict than the rules in this PR. So, I think it's probably worth landing this, since is better in terms of soundness.

However, I do think that my comments regarding user type annotations being effectively ignored should be addressed. It isn't critical for *correctness*, so *maybe* not worth blocking this PR on, but imo does provide a bad user experience so it's something I would *really* like to see before the PR lands.

body:
"qualif" is always an underapproximation: if it returns `true`, that means "maybe". If it returns `false`, that means "definitely not".

So when hitting a struct type, there are only two options:
- this type definitely does not qualify ("does not have the property we are checking for") on its own, but we need to check the fields. Return `false` from `in_adt_inherently`.
- this type might qualify on its own. Return `true`, which will propagate upwards and finish the computation, answering `true` overall.

Currently there is no way to encode "this type definitely does not qualify, no need to check the fields". But I don't think we have such a property.

Yeah, from what I can tell an operand bundle holds copies of the value pointers internally, so it would be unsound for the bundle to outlive those values.

Oh one other relevant point, `OperandBundleOwned` is closer to `Box<OperandBundle>`, since its representation is a pointer to the underlying bundle, and the owner is responsible for deallocating on drop.

body:
Hi! Sorry, I had to spend time building context back for myself as well. The whole story:

When trying to find if any trait provides an method or associated function, the resolver needs to keep all trait impls and their obligations in consideration. When evaluating something like `Ty::func()`, we will inject obligations coming from `Ty` with the `HirId` and `Span` corresponding to that `PathSegment`, like `Sized` or any of its `where`-bound clauses. Because `<str as From<&str>::from` doesn't exist, we hit that unmet obligation. So far this is the normal behavior.

In `suggest_add_reference_to_arg`, we try to identify expressions where the obligation isn't met for the found type, but is for the borrow of the found type. So if you have `foo(bar)` we suggest `foo(&mut bar)` if appropriate. But that logic kind of assumed that the source of the obligation was an expression, and not a path segment of a type relative path (like `Foo::bar`, as opposed to type absolute paths like `<Foo as Trait>::bar` or `<Foo>::bar`. Because of how rare this case was in our test suite, it seemed like the only situation where the logic I initially added would only ever trigger in a situation like `&Foo::bar()`, so it didn't seem necessary to make additional checks for the borrow actually being there (which is what was quite confusing of the code as written). The reason this "fixed" the issue was because by having the early return we ensured we didn't suggest the spurious `&`.

Looking at the changes and situation with fresh eyes, I noticed a couple of cases where we could hit that new logic in item signatures as well, so I added more checks (namely, the expected one that was missing) *and* added structured suggestions, as we now had all of the spans we needed for that.

I followed the example for `TlsModels`, since they seem of equivalent diagnostic value to me. For Android RISC-V targets TLSDESC is the default, and I *think* it may be a requirement.

> Also it should probably be made available on nightly only so we can remove it again once the traditional tls dialect is no longer used anywhere.

I'm not sure that will ever happen. TLSDESC requires support in the dynamic linker, so its imaginable that not all libcs will support that. For instance I've seen embedded targets that implement something like a loader service that support `__tls_get_addr` with overlays, but do not support TLSDESC.  

At any rate, I'm not sure we will ever drop support for traditional TLS in LLVM. It's been discussed, but I think its unlikely until GNU toolchains drop support.
author: ilovepi

body:
I'm OK w/ that, but I think its usually better to support an existing spelling when there are existing conventions in other compilers. We'd have to check w/ folks doing the GCC backend work, but its possible the variants would be easier to integrate for them.

We've talked about adding support for a 3 GOT slot variant of TLSDESC. That would require support from the linker and libc.  There are advantages to doing it that way, like avoiding a level of indirection to read the descriptor for the dynamic cases, but I'm not sure how likely that is to ever happen. I'd like to see it, and was hoping that would be the ABI for RISC-V, but it would be a win for any architecture.

But I can change this to a boolean if you'd like.

body:
I don't think that position is actually sustainable when it comes to codegen options. If we want to expose backend features like code coverage, sanitizers, and profiling, we have to accept that we don't control whether they continue to exist in all backends or continue to work in the same way with all the same knobs as before.

Of course there is always a balance to strike in terms of how much we expose and where the knobs should go. But we should prioritize giving users with minority needs the agency to solve their problems, ideally with tools that either work predictably or give you an error. I'm not sure backend options satisfy those criteria.

It might help to frame this as something more like a [target modifier](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3716). Support for targets – and by extension, target modifiers – is going to change over time and for different backends. It already does, as we have (correctly) promoted and demoted targets to different tiers based on concerns more myopic to the Rust project, such changing availability of hardware on which to run CI.

Target configurations and codegen options are all about integration across systems: The application, the compiler, the backend, the runtime, the operating system and the hardware it runs on. I do think we should document very clearly that support for this option, or other options like it, depend on the other layers of the stack. Ultimately, users will have to weigh the risk of one of those being pulled out from under them.

In any case, this is for now just an unstable flag, and I think we have precedent for others like it, so I don't think the higher level discussion should block this PR from merging. Perhaps we should continue this thread in Zulip or in another issue somewhere.

> I'm not sure how you can make that determination, since you can't know which libc someone is using ahead of time. Being able to configure and opt in/out is necessary, IMO.

Yes, you do. If you use x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu you know for sure that you are using glibc and in particular either the version we document as minimum supported version or newer. Once we document a version that supports TLSDESC as minimum supported version we can make TLSDESC enabled by defaulr for this target. The same applies for all other targets. Every target has exactly one libc implementation that is allowed to be used with it.

author: the8472

body:
> If there is a chance that LLVM ever drops the option, then no, we should not expose the option.

AFAIK, LLVM has no plans to drop support. Its hard to say *never*, but as a mater of practicality, I doubt it will be removed any time soon. If it does, we'd probably have a long period where its listed as "deprecated". Even then its possible it wouldn't actually be removed. There is precedent for that.

> There will be options to pass arguments directly to codegen backends, and if those suffice, then great, but otherwise we should resist getting into the habit of gaslighting our users by tricking them into thinking they have power and then not being able to fulfill their requests later because of the whims of those codegen backends.

In general, passing `-mllvm` options often fails for LTO builds, because frontends tend to fail to pass those along correctly to the linker via `-Wl,-mllvm,-option`. This was  particularly painful for RISC-V targets whose target features were not propagated to the linker correctly, and required extra build plumbing to solve.  It's arguably a failing of LLVM for not encoding those options in the IR. How to solve this class of problems has been being discussed for a long time now, and I don't think we'll arrive at a solution any time soon.

> It would be good to spell those out.

First, this comment was about compiler options in general. Defaults are usually chosen to make sense for the most common software. Projects may want to leverage knowledge they have about their system to improve performance, security, reduce size, etc.  It's quite hard to guess what requirements people may have, and failing to expose options that allows them to deviate from the default feels like the wrong approach for a compiler. 

For TLS dialects, I'd say performance is the most obvious motivation.  Another thing to consider is that you may want to support different configurations for the same target triple. For instance, Android after some particular SDK version may want to drop TLSDESC support, but you may need to retain the ability to target earlier SDKs that predate TLSDESC support in bionic. Similarly, we know that Fuchsia's driver ABI will only support TLSDESC, but the rest of the system will likely be more flexible about supporting both TLSDESC and traditional TLS.

Is Android planning to drop support for not using TLSDESC before the last LTS NDK that doesn't support TLSDESC is no longer supported? We only support the most recent LTS NDK.

> Similarly, we know that Fuchsia's driver ABI will only support TLSDESC, but the rest of the system will likely be more flexible about supporting both TLSDESC and traditional TLS.

author: bjorn3

body:
>  It's quite hard to guess what requirements people may have, and failing to expose options that allows them to deviate from the default feels like the wrong approach for a compiler.

This argument generalizes too much. It could mean that every single decision the compiler could make should have a user-facing option.

Compiler flags are part of our user interface. Which means they need testing, we need to consider compatibility, ABI unsoundness, terrible linker errors and so on. So adding one should come with a stronger motivation than "it'd be nice to have a knob, even though there's no immediate need".

As bjorn says it's possible that this decision is better left to a combination of target specifications and the compiler checking if it's supported (e.g. based on LLVM version) and determining the correct setting based on that.
