body: We currently [have a fallback](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/a31c5bfb6427afd162f554e48711829bf100f40f/compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/error_reporting/traits/suggestions.rs#L456-L483) where regardless of what the predicate that failed, we end up suggesting a bound ([with weasel wording that there might be a better way](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/5b542866400ad4a294f468cfa7e059d95c27a079/tests/ui/associated-types/issue-38821.stderr#L14-L17)). This is in place because there are [some](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/41e8d152dc5abb5a706999ada8b059d3420af8f3/tests/ui/associated-types/issue-85103-layout-debug.stderr) [complex](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/41e8d152dc5abb5a706999ada8b059d3420af8f3/tests/ui/suggestions/restrict-type-not-param.stderr) ([if uncommon](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/41e8d152dc5abb5a706999ada8b059d3420af8f3/tests/ui/associated-types/issue-85103-layout-debug.stderr)) bounds that are still useful to have that were given only by that. But in #104089, we had a report of that fallback doing the wrong thing (obvious in retrospect). The predicate might be something like `Self: From<T>`, where the `T` is a param *only in the associated item* and not at the `trait`/`impl` level. That's what this additional check guards against: If any part of the predicate references one of the generics of that item, we don't skip suggesting the bound at that level because it would be invalid in the parent item.

author: saethlin

body:
Thanks for taking a look!
I added comments to the functions, let me know if that makes it clearer or if you think something is unclear or missing.

To the point you mentioned here, `static_addr_of_impl` always returns a `llvm::GlobalVariable`. But that may not be a `ptr` (in LLVM IR; this is implicitly an `addrspace(0) ptr`, 0 is the default and is omitted), but a `addrspace(1) ptr`.
When we use a global in Rust (or in the ssa codegen), we need it to be just a `ptr` (so, `addrspace(0)`). Therefore, `static_addr_of` must return a `ptr` and it does that by inserting an `addrspacecast` on the result of `static_addr_of_impl`.

So, depending on what we need either function is called. If we need a `llvm::GlobalVariable`, we need to call `static_addr_of_impl`, if a `ptr` is needed, we call `static_addr_of`.

In https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/089bd510cf5ac835f1c3755f44fa2d15d211f09a/src/bootstrap/src/core/builder/mod.rs#L403, a step is skipped only if *all* of its pathsets and aliases are skipped, which seems quite suspicious to me, that makes some default steps really hard to skip.

body:
@workingjubilee the kernel validates the BTF info as part of calling `bpf_program_load`. Producing valid BTF right now means... generating whatever clang generates for C code. Non-C symbols in type names are not allowed (eg `<` in `Foo<u8>`), and there are some other annoying constraints.

@bjorn3 we discussed implementing BTF relocs on zulip a couple of years ago. Long term, you're correct it requires explicit rustc support if only because what debuginfo rustc generates with `-C debuginfo` is unspecified, so going from DI => relocs is fragile. In the meantime we think we can _probably_ hack it up in bpf-linker tho.

author: bjorn3

body:
The default response to upstreaming changes - even a lot less invasive than changing the calling convention - so far has been "if clang and the kernel don't need it, it doesn't belong to the target". Then there's the issue that the verifier would have to be made aware too, or `Fn(u8, u8, u8, u8, u8)` and `Fn(u8, u8, u8, u8, u8, u8)` would look like the same type to it. But nothing in the kernel uses more than 5 args, so the chance of getting that merged seems very slim too.

Technically yes this is a very easy thing to fix (and in fact at work we have a LLVM fork that already does all this and more), but socially it's much harder (and at work we've given up on upstreaming).

body:
> by `layout_of_struct_or_enum` which returns `LayoutCalculatorError::UnexpectedUnsized`, would you like to handle this as `TooGeneric` as well?

No, `UnexpectedUnsized` has nothing to do with generics at all.

My idea behind `LayoutError::TooGeneric` is that this error means that the layout cannot be computed, because it depends on some generic type parameter `T` that has not been instantiated yet.

For example

```rust
fn foo<T>() {
    [(); size_of::<T>()];
 /*                ^ the layout of the type parameter `T` cannot be computed,
                     therefore the constant `size_of::<T>()` cannot be evaluated */ 
}
```

And `LayoutError::Unknown` would be a catch-all, like it currently is. So for example if we attempt to compute the layout of `(str, str)` that would return `LayoutError::Unknown`. Or if the layout computation fails for some other reason that is not further specified, that would return `LayoutError::Unknown`.

The semantic difference between the two would be that `LayoutError::TooGeneric` means that the layout may become available if the type parameters are further instantiated, i.e. in the example above if we called `foo::<i32>()` then the layout of the `T` will become known, but `LayoutError::Unknown` always means "this type is broken, the layout is meaningless".

Then we can map `LayoutError::TooGeneric` to `ErrorHandled::TooGeneric` here: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3323bbec7ed62974b3f0b1b7fd05f93ed7945259/compiler/rustc_const_eval/src/const_eval/error.rs#L143-L145
This const eval error basically means "we cannot evaluate this constant because there are uninstantiated generic parameters" and the layout error `TooGeneric` would mean the same.

On the contrary, `LayoutError::Unknown` would fall through to the error reporting case below and actually report the error, because no further monomorphization can save us: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3323bbec7ed62974b3f0b1b7fd05f93ed7945259/compiler/rustc_const_eval/src/const_eval/error.rs#L152-L176

At the same time the new `LayoutError::TooGeneric` would also be used instead of `LayoutError::Unknown` in the `SizeSkeleton`, which is used to typecheck `transmute`: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/243d2ca4db6f96d2d18aaf3a2381251d38eb6b0b/compiler/rustc_middle/src/ty/layout.rs#L353

And for checking the CMSE function signatures for generic parameters: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/243d2ca4db6f96d2d18aaf3a2381251d38eb6b0b/compiler/rustc_hir_analysis/src/hir_ty_lowering/cmse.rs#L204

All so that we can discern layout errors due to "this type has generics" vs "this type in invalid".

---

> Maybe we should introduce a new variant to `LayoutCalculatorError`?

The layout calculator is more low-level than the `layout_of_uncached` function and does the actual layout computation algorithm. It only knows very basic types (scalars/ADTs) and is unaware of generics (type parameters) for example. The `LayoutCalculatorError` enum is for errors that stem from the layout optimizing algorithm itself, so adding a new variant there doesn't really seem appropiate.

body:
Ah, sorry, I understand what you mean now. Yeah my idea is that just `ty::Param` & `ty::Alias` (if the alias has a param) are handled as `TooGeneric` and all other `LayoutError::Unknown` will stay the same -- including the one from `LayoutCalculatorError::UnexpectedUnsized`.

Currently, we convert all `LayoutError::Unknown` (which can happen for various reasons, and not just the type being "too generic") to the const eval error `ErrorHandled::TooGeneric` and only report the other variants of `LayoutError` as "failed to evaluate constant" errors. The idea with `LayoutError::TooGeneric` is that now *only* layout errors from `ty::Param` & `ty::Alias` that are actually "too generic" (in the sense that they contain generic type parameters) are mapped to `ErrorHandled::TooGeneric` and all remaining `LayoutError::Unknown`s, including the one from `LayoutCalculatorError::UnexpectedUnsized` should then be reported as "failed to evaluate constant" errors.

So if you implement `LayoutError::TooGeneric` like that, then you will fix https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/135138 without using `LayoutError::TooGeneric` for `LayoutCalculatorError::UnexpectedUnsized` (which has nothing to do with generics).

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3323bbec7ed62974b3f0b1b7fd05f93ed7945259/compiler/rustc_monomorphize/src/collector.rs#L654-L665

**Argumenting the second point of the previous comment**

The infinite recursion originates in the following function:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3323bbec7ed62974b3f0b1b7fd05f93ed7945259/compiler/rustc_monomorphize/src/collector.rs#L355-L356

Specifically, this line appears to be problematic:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3323bbec7ed62974b3f0b1b7fd05f93ed7945259/compiler/rustc_monomorphize/src/collector.rs#L468 

---

`eval_constant` function returns an `Option`, and the `None` variant is being ignored. This makes it difficult to see what is described in the comment. To address this, the compilation process should abort in such cases to avoid unexpected behavior.
Consider this section of the code:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3323bbec7ed62974b3f0b1b7fd05f93ed7945259/compiler/rustc_monomorphize/src/collector.rs#L1237-L1243

The `items_of_instance` function is only used in `collect_items_rec`. It would be more robust to have it explicitly report an `Option` where `None` indicates if an error occurs during the visit. This would allow the recursion to be stopped immediately when an error is encountered.

--- 

This could be done in another PR, but this one would still fail

body:
> The `items_of_instance` function is only used in `collect_items_rec`. It would be more robust to have it explicitly report an `Option` where `None` indicates if an error occurs during the visit. This would allow the recursion to be stopped immediately when an error is encountered.

This sounds reasonable, but please use `Result<T,` [`ErrorGuaranteed`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_errors/struct.ErrorGuaranteed.html) `>` rather than `Option<T>` with `None` for the error case. There should be a `ErrorGuaranteed` in the const eval error.
author: lukas-code

body:
> The error reporting appears to be working perfectly fine, but we should probably abort after enough errors have been reported rather than go on forever.
> 

Yes, the reporting is correct. The problem is that it simply does not terminate.

Sure, changing the `Option<T>` to `Result<T, ErrorGuaranteed>` here should be fine, as long as you keep the commits somewhat separate (and squash all your fixups of adding `LayoutError::TooGeneric` into a single commit).

There can be four cases here:

- the const failed to evaluate, i.e. `count` is a `ConstKind::Error` -> here we should return `LayoutError::ReferencesError` with the ErrorGuaranteed from the const and not `LayoutError::TooGeneric`
- the const evaluated successfully, i.e. `count` is a `ConstKind::Value` and fits in a target usize -> all good

And then instead of `lower_assoc_path_shared` calling `probe_inherent_assoc_shared`/`lower_assoc_shared` and the callers, `lower_assoc_path_ty/const` constructing the `Ty`/`Const`, we match inside of `lower_assoc_path_shared` in order to call the `_shared` version of iat probing and assoc path lowering.

- Remove `probe_inherent_assoc_ty/const` and `lower_assoc_ty/const`
- Have `lower_assoc_path_shared` call the `_shared` versions of such functions
- Have `lower_assoc_path_ty/const` construct the `ConstKind::Unevaluated`/`TyKind::Alias` from the defid + args pair in `LoweredAssoc::Term`

Right now things feel a bit "inside out" where the `_shared` functions attempt to do logic that isnt actually shared and is special between types/consts and then erase the fact that it did this by returning a `Type` or `Const` variant, instead of having the caller handle the bits special to types vs consts and bubbling up the information necessary to construct the `Ty`/`Const`

body:
Actually, it's not the straightforward undertaking we were imagining, so I probably won't have the time to do it soon:
- this is not just used as simple bitset here, but with bitrelations to other bitsets
- the cartesian product of the bitrelations on these different bitset types is not complete, and some of the existing implementation is apparently for a subset of cases. Basically, the easy cases seem done, where domain sizes match (and that's enough in most cases so it makes sense).
- otherwise changing the bitset type here would require changing it upstream in storage liveness, locals live across awaits in coroutines analysis, the coroutine storage analysis and conflicts and their own bitmatrices, and so on. That may be an improvement to these other parts in turn, but it's not clear, given we have no data that this happens on large numbers of locals yet. As an example, only 1 primary benchmark exercises the `MaybeStorageLive` analysis (38 times, with the domains always being <=350, whereas the `MixedBitSet` cutoff is 2048). rustc/libstd also hits this very little (20 or so, always under the cutoff). As of now we only have data where these are used as dense bitsets anyways and wouldn't benefit from the new representation.
- the domain sizes should work out if these are always on locals, but I don't know if that's always the case for all these other related computations (some of the coroutine locals are renumbered over saved locals, so these won't have the same domain size for example).

Overall, this currently looks like a cold path, and since we have no benchmarks that would be improved, I suggest we wait until the benchmarks update of 2025 to see if the ecosystem is now more reliant on this. Then we can reassess with this new dataset, and then do that big chunk work if needed.

body: Maybe differentiating the assignments generated from lowering argument patterns to where they are lowered instead would still allow to do this diagnostics improvement at a lower cost -- or the opposite, using the same method but on the error path, where we know it's not as perf-sensitive.
author: lqd

body:
Unfortunately, using the same method only on the error path doesn't seem clean to me, at least in the general case. The constraint category is used by `best_blame_constraint`, which runs during borrowck on the happy path when outlives constraints from closures need to be propagated to whatever body they're defined in. We could maybe track in `best_blame_constraint` whether we're emitting an error or checking a closure, but we'd risk not blaming a propagated outlives constraint from a closure if it happened to be from an argument pattern. There's already a bit of weirdness with not blaming ideal constraints when they're propagated from closures, so I'd rather not make that more confusing.

Differentiating assignments during lowering would work, I think. I'd looked into putting the information in the assignment's span (as a new kind of desugaring) to avoid needing to store anything extra in the MIR itself. I opted not to go for that though since it looked like keeping track of which assignments came from argument patterns would require an unpleasant amount of bookkeeping during either MIR or THIR construction. It wouldn't be hard, but the added complexity didn't seem worth it to me for such a niche diagnostic tweak[^1]. I don't think I checked how much bookkeeping it'd be to do elsewhere, though.

Another option would be to give up (for now) on preventing assignments from argument patterns from being blamed, and instead just pick a different name for assignments (like "binding", maybe[^2]) when they're syntactically not from assignment-like syntax. This should be doable entirely on the error path, and would also mean we could avoid calling match expressions "assignments" too if we'd like.

We could also try an entirely different heuristic to hopefully better address the issue this hack was papering over (see the footnote below) but it'd be a substantial enough change that it should have its own PR, and I'm honestly not confident the fix I have in mind would work. There might be some other less-fragile/hacky way of writing `best_blame_constraint` altogether, but I'm not sure how if so. borrowck as written makes it difficult to tell exactly why region errors occur, hence the need for `best_blame_constraint` to divine some meaning.

I'm not sure which of these options would be best to pursue, but I think just picking a different word for assignments from argument patterns (and maybe also match expressions) would be easiest and least intrusive.

[^1]: I *think* the argument pattern is only being blamed here instead of the more relevant assignment in the function body because of how we handle invariance in diagnostics. The main trick `best_blame_constraint` uses to guess what to blame for region errors breaks down when the regions involved are related contravariantly, and we currently don't have a reliable way of knowing when that's the case. Hence all the heuristics like that one to try and blame something hopefully-reasonable even in those cases.

[^2]: I'm not totally sure on what word would be best. The nice thing about "assignment" is it's very clear about the relationship being described.

LGTM. Sorry for taking a bit to review this.

I don't believe this needs an FCP, because it simply fixes a shortcoming in vtable validation code -- this is *morally* equivalent[^1] to changing the `eq_in_param_env` function to instantiate the binder of the principal trait ref (à la #135318) and then performing a [leak check](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_infer/infer/region_constraints/struct.RegionConstraintCollector.html#method.leak_check) at the end of processing obligations. 

The fact that we weren't previously leak-checking (or equivalent) allows certain kinds of transmutes to pass miri today that clearly allow changing the principal trait ref in a way that constitutes different types (e.g. `fn(&'static ())` and `for<'a> fn(&'a ())`).

[^1]: Though simpler b/c we don't need to actually go through the whole dance of using an infcx if we expect the types to be fully normalized and region erased.

author: tgross35

body:
That's very intentional.  As I see it, the semantic meaning of `-> SomeType` is "how do I get `SomeType`".  While a pure functional builder pattern does not technically mutate, it is not a satisfactory answer to "how do i get the thing".

Also remember that:
1. We're not filtering them out, only ranking them lower.  For simple types that have few methods, they're still easily accessible.
2. result sorting is a zero-sum game, something has to go at the bottom, and something has to go at the top.

However, `Default::default` is intentionally *not* deprioritized, as it *is* a reasonable answer to "how do i get the thing", and in some crates, it may be the only constructor.

Hope this clears things up :]

body: Can you explain this more in the commit message? Why do we want a "raw" version that returns `Box<[u16]>` instead of always using `OsString`?
author: nicholasbishop

body:
I have added the details to the commit message, but to explain in short, to open files in UEFI, we need to do 2 open requests:
1. Volume
2. File inside volume

To perform this, we need to compare the `EFI_DEVICE_PATH_NODE`s in a device path with all the volumes found in the system and open the one that matches. Then we take there remaining `EFI_DEVICE_PATH_PROTOCOL`, convert it to UTF-16 and pass that to `EFI_FILE_PROTOCOL->Open` to open the actual file/directory. 

If using `OsString`, we would need to go from `EFI_DEVICE_PATH` -> `OsString` (WTF-8 internally) -> UTF-16. The extra conversion to `OsString` (and extra allocation) is not required in this case since we already know that the path is a valid UTF-16 path (since it is created by UEFI device path to text representation), and does not need validation again. Also, this intermediate remaining path is never used on std side again, so it makes sense to avoid the round conversion.

Basically, this allows removing 2 intermediate allocations and 2 unnecessary validation for the File APIs.

Note, the string returned by `EFI_DEVICE_PATH_TO_TEXT` is owned by the caller (Rust code), so the only difference here is that we are returning the UTF-16 string as is, instead of performing conversion to WTF-8, and silently freeing up the UTF-16 string.
author: Ayush1325

body:
`Box::from_raw` doesn't look quite right to me. If I'm understanding the usage correctly, the input `ptr` is coming from a raw UEFI allocation. E.g.  `convert_device_path_to_text` is going to allocate with `AllocatePool`, and must be freed with `FreePool`. [`Box::from_raw`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#method.from_raw) requires that the memory must be allocated with the [memory layout](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/index.html#memory-layout) used by `Box`. Per those docs, "It is valid to convert both ways between a [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html) and a raw pointer allocated with the [Global](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/alloc/struct.Global.html) allocator", so the details then depend on the allocator, which I think is [`r-efi-alloc`](https://github.com/r-efi/r-efi-alloc/blob/main/src/raw.rs) in this case. Internally that does use `AllocatePool`/`FreePool`, but with various size and alignment tweaks to satisfy Layout requirements. From a quick read, I'm not sure if this will end up having exactly the same layout as raw Allocate/Free calls in the end or not. If it is correct, then this line needs a much more detailed safety comment, and if not then we'd need to reallocate anyway.

`os_string_from_raw` doesn't have this issue, since `OsString::from_wide` takes a slice and does it's own internal allocation. I think it might be better to stick with using that. You're right that there will be some extra conversion overhead, but I think it would be premature optimization to try and avoid that right now. Better to get the APIs implemented with minimal `unsafe` shenanigans, get testing enabled, and then -- if profiling shows it's worth it -- look into optimizing.
author: nicholasbishop

body:
While I am not opposed to going back to using OsString, let me iterate what guarantees UEFI and r-efi-alloc makes:

The pointer allocated on UEFI side will always be 8 byte aligned, nothing less nothing more. It is the same for all targets as well, not just x86_64.

`r-efi-alloc` will do nothing special for `alignment <= 8` and will just behave as if `AllocatePool / FreePool` are directly used.

I am a bit iffy regarding what alignment `Box<[u8]>` has, though. In my testing, it seems be 8, and should not be higher than 8, but if we cannot prove that the exact alignment will be <= 8, then it can lead to UB.

author: bjorn3

body:
I think what you're pointing out here is that these functions are not reachable _as MIR_, so we don't need to encode MIR for them. The problem as I see it is that our notion of reachable uses this worklist/visited algorithm that tracks items in a path-independent way: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/2ae9916816a448fcaab3b2da461de754eda0055a/compiler/rustc_passes/src/reachable.rs#L168-L173

Also we already have an issue for the inverse inefficiency, emitting object code when we only need MIR: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/119214

I put a hack in this place specifically because the compiler is designed around this function either true or false for whatever reason, past the first few checks. I'm not aware of anywhere else we could make a small localized change to get the behavior we want.

The only other place I could think of putting a hack is `MonoItem::instantiation_mode`, but that doesn't work because then we get linker errors because instantiation mode needs to agree with `exported_symbols`, and those disagree because because `exported_symbols` is based on `reachable_set`. I really think the inaccuracy of the `reachable_set` analysis is the root problem here, and it's net better to implement this in a non-invasive way that will be fixed automatically if `reachable_set` gets improved.

body:
Actually, I have no idea what you're asking for here. In the situation that you call a function with unsatisfied const conditions:

1. The `const_trait_impl` feature gate is enabled, then we report an error in HIR. This exists only as a sanity check so we detect cases where `~const` predicates are not checked in the type checker.
2. The gate is not enabled, in which case we report a `ConditionallyConstCall` error later on, which is gated on the `const_trait_impl` feature gate.

In the latter case, we don't want to mention what `~const` predicate does not hold if we don't even have the `const_trait_impl` feature gate enabled. Users of stable rust should not be concerned with const predicates.

For enums that are passed across FFI to C/C++ code, we shouldn't delete Rust-side variants that are unused.

Yeah, please add it back to both.

(Our `LLVMRustDebugNameTableKind` enum is basically just a substitute for LLVM's `DICompileUnit::DebugNameTableKind`. body:
The unresumed variant was not overlapping the upvars before, but I would like to make this change to the classical layout to preserve the uniformity in MIR and codegen.

Previously, upvars as prefix fields `_1.$n` are not ambiguous. Whether the MIR is at the CTFE stage or runtime-optimised stage, projecting out of `_1` will always get us upvars. When we relocate upvars to the unresumed variant, this notation gets trickier. For instance, the MIR validation does not care if the coroutine MIR is before or after `StateTransform` pass and, if we change validation to also consider coroutine layout scheme, it would either need to do simple field projection `_1.$n` or reinterpret as `(_1 as variant 0).$n`. This change also applies to other parts of the MIR processes, such as codegen and const-eval.

So I decide to keep it simple and make the unresumed variant share the same memory region of the prefix under the classic style. On the MIR level, when projecting out upvars especially during CTFE, the classical style `_1.$n` it is reinterpreted as `(_1 as variant 0).$n`.

However, when the classical layout style is concerned, the memory layout stays the same and the generated code should be the same as well.

I think the size here is precisely `21` because there are 5 nested levels of `use_future` contributing one `i8` each.

The precise expected layout is
```
(i8, (i8, (i8, (i8, (i8, [u8; 16])))))
```

It would be a regression if this takes more than `21` bytes. There must be unnecessary padding or wasted space.

Optimising it down to `(i8, [u8; 16])` is on my wish list, if we could inline the intermediate coroutines and squash it into just one level. For now, `21` is the best we could do.

"natural alignment"?

What does "natural alignment" mean?

The alignment of f64 is 8 bytes, so the "natural alignment" of the struct should be 8 bytes, and the produced struct will be 8 bytes, but the [alignment to 4 bytes described here](https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/repr-c-aix-struct-alignment/21594) by @mustartt is not a "natural alignment".

body:
`DUMMY_SP` is does not just have a start and end with the same value, the value of them is `0`, which is reserved for "unknown".

Also, when the start and end of a span is to the same position, then the span is said to be pointing "between" `start - 1` and `start`, like a cursor does. When rendering, we point at `start` to `start + 1`. We can give the span a width of 1, but that might fail in some cases if the following byte is a multi-byte char. Given how niche this error should be in practice I wasn't inclined to spend too much time tweaking this output, and given how... "terse" the current output was, I wanted to have something finished earlier rather than later so that we could iterate on it on main (if needed).

body:
The check below for the path is also wrong

```
objdump -Wi $(TMPDIR)/foo | grep DW_AT_GNU_dwo_name | (grep $(TMPDIR)) || exit 1
```

because

```
[03:00] Joe:rust (migrate-split-debuginfo *%) | objdump -Wi foo | grep DW_AT_GNU_dwo_name -B 5 -A 5
objdump: Warning: Unable to load dwo file: /home/joe/repos/rust/foo.foo.fc848df41df7a00d-cgu.0.rcgu.dwo
   Abbrev Offset: 0x0
   Pointer Size:  8
 <0><b>: Abbrev Number: 1 (DW_TAG_compile_unit)
    <c>   DW_AT_stmt_list   : 0x0
    <10>   DW_AT_comp_dir    : (indirect string, offset: 0xafb48): /home/joe/repos/rust
    <14>   DW_AT_GNU_dwo_name: (indirect string, offset: 0x5d1b0): foo.foo.fc848df41df7a00d-cgu.0.rcgu.dwo
    <18>   DW_AT_GNU_dwo_id  : 0x17249573aa475dc7
    <20>   DW_AT_low_pc      : 0x0
    <28>   DW_AT_ranges      : 0x0
    <2c>   DW_AT_GNU_addr_base: 0x0
  Compilation Unit @ offset 0x30:
```

`DW_AT_GNU_dwo_name`'s attribute value is the `.dwo` (or object) file name `foo.foo.fc848df41df7a00d-cgu.0.rcgu.dwo`, **not** the containing path `/home/joe/repos/rust` which is the attr value of `DW_AT_comp_dir`. So this check is not checking what it thinks it's checking.

body:
> but with verbatim we can just pass the -l:libfoo.so.1 to the linker and it will pick that up for the NEEDED so name.

What if the user passes an absolute path as verbatim name? `NEEDED` entries accept absolute paths just fine, but `-l:` would look at the wrong location. `SONAME` can encode arbitrary values to set as `NEEDED` without messing up the search logic of the linker. Also using `SONAME` + random filename for the stub library should still allow `#[link(name = "foo")]` to still look for the system libfoo.so even if there is a `#[link_name = "foo", kind = "raw-dylib")]` only encodes a subset of the functions available in libfoo.so (as the crate in question didn't need the rest). If the stub library is called `libfoo.so` it would take precedence over the system install and thus every raw-dylib block would need to exhaustively list all functions, including those not needed by the crate in question to avoid breaking someones build.

body: This file is infrastructure that I think should replace `rustc_ast/attr/mod.rs` some day. Right now it is some duplication, unfortunately. The types and methods here make it much easier to parse attributes correctly. It allows you to more often exhaustively match on attributes, making sure no cases are forgotten. Importantly, it is made to get information out of attributes. The functions in `rustc_ast/attr/mod.rs` are just to break up an attribute into MetaItems, which are still just essentially TokenStreams. The result is that these unparsed or half-parsed MetaItems are passed around all the time. I realise this adds some code now. Soon I think we can completely delete `rustc_ast/attr/mod.rs` which might make up for it. But to me, this really is quite an important change in this PR. This is what makes it easier to parse attributes correctly.
author: jdonszelmann

body: I've also tried to document it well. The goal was to make it easy and clear to use, well documented, and to make it so there is one obvious way to parse attributes instead of around 10, everyone doing it slightly differently. In some way this is an n+1th standard, like the xkcd, but it enables us to remove `rustc_ast/attr/mod.rs`.

body:
I think we should mention the established term *inert (attributes)* here.

Not getting expanded isn't an inherent quality of *built-in* attributes which this paragraph seems to convey (I might be wrong) [but of *inert* ones as opposed to *active* ones](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes.html#active-and-inert-attributes). Note that we do have active built-in attributes — see `LegacyAttr`.

Further, inert doesn't imply built-in: [Proc-macro helper attributes](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html#derive-macro-helper-attributes) are also considered to be inert (of course, they don't live quite as long as built-in inert ones as they don't survive macro expansion).

body:
Maybe we can have a macro just for the pattern part, but a method on the attr list (or wherever) that is easily discoverable?
```rust
attrs.find_attr(|a| nonexhaustive_match!(a, AttributeKind::Repr(r) => r))
```
The `find_attr` docs would recommend this pattern.
Here, `nonexhaustive_match!(e, pat => expr)` is
```rust
match e {
  pat => Some(expr),
  _ => None,
}
```
 The name `nonexhaustive_match` is terrible obviously, but up to that I think this is easier to discover and avoids a lot of the magic of `find_attr!`. (If we really want a shortcut for avoiding `is_some()`, that could be a separate method.)

body:
I *could* do that, it just feels like a worse fit here.

This isn't like these intrinsics

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/a30f9151fe4a841c4643af4e47ad18a23e1fb044/compiler/rustc_codegen_llvm/src/intrinsic.rs#L29-L154

where we're lowering it to some call, or the ones depending on LLVM-only integer types, or whatever.

It's far more like `add nuw`, where we have `add`, `unchecked_sadd`, and `unchecked_uadd` [on `BuilderMethods`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_codegen_ssa/traits/builder/trait.BuilderMethods.html#tymethod.unchecked_sadd), because it's an instruction in the IR and something that we can use in other places in MIR-to-Backend lowering.  (For example, we could use it in emitting rotates since we might as well and it's no less safe than the shifts that are also unchecked in the builder.)

And sure, those two unchecked examples don't have defaults today, but they should, because cg_gcc is just emitting `self.gcc_add(a, b)` for all three anyway, and if we want cg_ssa to be useful it shouldn't require implementing these when there's perfectly fine -- albeit potentially suboptimal -- provided implementations.

body: I realize this talk about leaves is taken from #134088 but it doesn't reflect how `BTreeMap` works. *All* nodes (leaf and interior nodes) contain an array of elements and search may terminate in any them, not just in leaves. That's also closer to how binary search trees usually work. B+ trees, a variant of the traditional B-tree, do the "only leaves store elements, interior nodes guide search to the right leaf" thing but Rust's `BTree*` types are not like that.
author: hanna-kruppe

body: This may just be collateral damage from the leaves vs interior distinction, but it seems strange to only mention the linear search for leaves. The current implementation does it for every node, if it's mentioned for one it should be mentioned for both. Alternatively, it may be considered an implementation detail that distracts from the main point (logarithmic time complexity w.r.t. total number of elements, despite linear search in each node). But then it shouldn't be mentioned for leaves either. Certainly the way each node is searched is less central to the mechanical sympathy of B-trees than the "B" constant: fewer and larger nodes are obviously good (up to a point), while linear vs binary search is a more nuanced decision.
author: hanna-kruppe

body:
If you do want to salvage e.g. a brief mention of fewer nodes with more elements being better for reducing heap allocations and cache misses, consider this suggestions from https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/134088#issuecomment-2530463172

> If we do wish to explain the theory behind B-tree performance, we can do it near the end, when we are not crushed for time and space.
author: hanna-kruppe

body:
I agree with @workingjubilee (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/134088#issuecomment-2530463172) that

> our first primary goal is not to explain "why not BinarySearchTreeMap?" We don't have a BinarySearchTreeMap, but we do have HashMap, so our first task is "why should you EVER look at this data structure and not HashMap?" This is true even if we never directly compare, in the type's docs, against HashMap.

So while you're already condensing the existing description, do you think you could also include this aspect? Essentially, say more about this being an "ordered map" before diving into *how* it maintains order internally.

Yes, this is definitely collateral damage from my faulty guessing at the internal workings. I guess I was too hasty dismissing this possibility as not being compatible with logarithmic behavior, but I see now that I was wrong. Thanks for clarifying.
I don't agree about larger nodes being obviously good. I think it has more to do with the minimum number of bits that a real machine can look at, due to the size of its cache lines or some other detail. If your algorithm uses smaller chunks, then it is wasting bandwidth. So I would say smaller is obviously better (since it gets you from linear search to logarithmic search), but only up to a point.

author: hanna-kruppe

body:
In the context of comparison against BST, anything more than one key per node is a "larger node". You're right that the granularity of memory/storage access (cache lines in main memory, block/page size for disks) is a useful rule of thumb. Larger nodes also make *insertion and deletion* more expensive. But you're mistaken about search complexity: as the existing comments note, you can maintain optimal number of comparisons (up to a small constant factor) by doing binary search in each node. Sometimes that turns out a bit slower than a linear search, but it's competitive or superior in other cases.

In any case, I don't think it's useful to try and communicate these nuances in the `BTreeMap` docs.
